en: Preface to the Recorded Sayings of Master Shouchang:
In the past, the World-Honored One expounded the net of the Three Vehicles to rescue and guide those among devas and humans. At the very end, he held up a flower to show the assembly;
only the Venerable Kāśyapa was able to accept this transmission. It was as if the Buddha had handed over the precious sword of the Vajra King to Kāśyapa, who then—
You wield it recklessly and employ it perversely; you can kill and you can bring to life. Yet, in the end, its sharp edge is never revealed, for it is withdrawn and kept within its sheath.
Thus, one who truly upholds this Way merely breaks into a smile.

Since that time, the succession has been passed down through the various patriarchs of India and China, all of whom have likewise grasped this Vajra King to sever the life-roots of countless people throughout the past and present.

He was always one who would draw his sword to aid others whenever he encountered injustice on the road. Alas! The ancestral temple lies in ruin and desolation; the Way of the Dharma has declined and fallen into decay.

This sword has long been buried, and who now shall pluck this flower? Unless there is one who transcends the standards and measures of past and present, how could anyone else be worthy of such a heavy responsibility?
Master Shouchang’s spiritual influence suppresses the ancients, his iron will supports the heavens, and he wondrously attained the state of teacherless realization.
Therefore, he bestowed these Dharma words, which are authentically natural; their application is sovereign, devoid of any talk of forced effort or contrived exclusion.
Their seams and threads are so dense that they attain the subtle wonder of the interplay between the partial and the perfect.
Having overturned the old molds and cast off all lingering attachments, who other than this Master could be one who, in the age of the Final Dharma, skillfully wields the Vajra King Sword? Thus...
The filial and incorruptible Mr. Deng had long admired his writings. A verse he composed reads: "The Wild Master does not eat the food of the human world;
Upon the twelve peaks of Wu, he has attained freedom. Having cultivated the power of unimpeded mastery, He turns Mount Kunlun upside down to become the Isle of Yingzhou.

Upon reading this, [Deng] joyfully said, "Who would have expected that as I approach old age, I might drink the *tīrtha* (the essence of enlightenment)? Were it not for one who has truly practiced and realized awakening, how could one compare with the Buddhas and Patriarchs?"
The vital pulse flows freely, streaming forth from within one’s own breast. How could it be otherwise? To what extent is its essence profound!

In the past, Lingyuan said that Master Duoxi did not flatter nor was he vulgar; he remarked that his natural endowment accorded with the Way and that his speech and silence were measured by the middle way.
Now, this Master shares the same spirit as Master Yan, though they lived in different eras. Indeed, his solitary standard and the resonance of his Way stand out preeminent.

How extraordinary! Like ten-thousand-fathom peaks rising from the void, their ridges stand as if turned upside down; his upright mind and straightforward conduct were like an arrow hitting the bullseye.

His countenance was solemn and majestic, devoid of even a trace of vulgarity or arrogance. Thus, for over fifty years since he took up residence on the mountain, his footsteps never trod upon city walls or moats, nor did he approach the gates of the wealthy or powerful with letters or petitions.
He possessed the spirit of profound seclusion found at Damei; only it is a pity that such a person has not appeared in this world.
Master Mashizi. Who would have known that his plum had been ripe for so long? The Master once traveled to Shaolin and Mount Wutai, where he met Master Ruifeng.
At first sight, Ruifeng recognized him; they attained mutual accord, and Ruifeng held him in profound esteem. Day after day, he joined the assembly in manual labor.
Before the others had even reached the fields, the Master was already there with his spade. Though he braved the wind and endured the rain, he never showed the slightest sign of weariness.
Upon returning, he would adjust his robes, ascend the seat, and preach the Dharma for the assembly. He spoke spontaneously, beyond the reach of conceptual thought.

Those among the monastics who were fond of displaying their verbal acuity or relishing literary phrasing often regarded the Master’s Dharma words as if they were sipping soup made of wood shavings—lacking the flavor of minced meat or roasted delicacies.
Some even used this to criticize the Master; the Master, however, once laughed at such people, saying they were like the Duke of Ye, who was terrified of a true dragon.
Listen! Suppose we were to have him hear the words regarding "plowing fields to earn one's meal" at the same time as [hearing] those of Kṣitigarbha;

he would surely also claim that they do not accord with the profound principles of the Zen school. I privately believe that if this Master’s Dharma-words were placed alongside those of the great elders such as Xueyan and Gaofeng, they would not yield much ground to them.
There are those in the world who appreciate beauty; they would surely strike their palms in approval. Yet, such was the Master’s intent.
The essence lies in one’s conduct; strive to emulate the ancient style. Though one might stand shoulder-to-shoulder with Baizhang or Moshan, what cause for shame would there be?
His spiritual practices and hidden virtues are too numerous to enumerate; here, I shall describe their general outline.

As Confucius said, "I would rather see these things manifest in actual deeds than merely recorded as empty words. Thus, the Master cultivated both practice and understanding simultaneously, such that even when measured against the ancients...
How could there be any doubt regarding a Sage? At first, the Master resided at the two hermitages of E’feng and Bǎofāng; subsequently, he moved to Shòuchāng.
Shòuchāng was the site of the Dharma seat of the Western India Chan Master. Xīzhú was a native of Chóngrén and shared the same hometown as the Master.
There was a prophetic verse that said: "Shòuchāng loves to herd oxen; Xīzhú returns once more to roam. Not even ten days had passed since the Master arrived at Shòuchāng when...
The Brahma-realm monastery rose majestically; all people said that the Master was surely the reincarnation of the ancient Shouchang. This belief is likely not unfounded.
On the day the Buddha attained enlightenment in the year of Bingchen.
Respectfully inscribed by the disciple from Xinzhou, Liu Chongqing, at his hermitage on Mount Jinhua,
following the sequence of the Recorded Sayings of Master Wuming of Shouchang.
Volume One:
The Record of Sayings of E Peak; The Record of Sayings of Bao Fang; The Record of Sayings of Dongyan.
Volume Two.
Shouchang’s Recorded Sayings: Verses on Ancient Cases and Verses on Ancient Cases, Volume Three;
E’peak Questions and Answers; Praises.
Scroll Four:
Verses, Miscellaneous Writings, Epitaphs,
and the Recorded Sayings of Master Shouchang, Volume One.
Re-edited by the junior dharma-heir Yuanxian, residing at Yongquan Chan Monastery on Mount Gu in Fuzhou;
based on the records of the Master’s first stay at Mount E’feng, including the discourse for the opening of the hall.
Having finished the proclamation of the memorial, the presentation of incense, and the striking of the mallet, the Master again presented incense and asked, "Does the assembly understand?
This is that which the Buddhas of the three periods have never exhausted; I now cast it all at once toward the Sahā world.
Even Śākyamuni Buddha has not yet exhausted its use, nor have the successive patriarchs of India and this land exhausted its use. Today, I, this mountain monk..."
Picking it up with the hand of faith to deliberate with the assembly: Is this the separate transmission outside the teachings, the profound purport within the scriptures?

Does it encompass heaven and earth while following the waves? Does it cut off the myriad streams and raise it up for deliberation? Is it the great function manifest before one, like a probing pole or a blade of grass?
Is it the Vajra-treasure sword cast out in the open? To discuss this according to reality to its ultimate limit—how could there be any further words?
The kalpas will not end; one must possess the eye of wisdom to discern and distinguish them clearly—white as white and black as black—so that they are not lumped together as a single mass.
Only then can the right and wrong of the monastic community be settled and the success or failure of practitioners be verified.
Whether responding to the holy or the mundane, one will naturally not be deceived by those who feign enlightenment. In all actions and responses to conditions, there shall be no error.
This is not auspicious. However, this Way is subtle and profound, having been neglected for a long time.

Among the assembly, those of great wisdom should be prepared to sacrifice their very lives and exert all their strength to support and uphold it, taking awakening as their goal. To benefit both self and others, one lifetime may not suffice;

one must be prepared to sacrifice another lifetime, and at most three lifetimes, until it is inevitably attained. As the ancients said: "Without entering the great ocean of birth and death, it is difficult [to attain the Way]."
"Obtaining a priceless jewel"—this still refers to those of dull faculties. A clever person knows its wondrousness upon hearing it once.
Nevertheless, even so, without the spring breeze, the flowers will not bloom. Let us speak for a moment: yet when the flowers do bloom, they are blown away by the wind.

The Head Seat stepped forth from the assembly and asked: "Before you have bestowed your Dharma words, you have already entered into prolixity. Please briefly borrow words of expedient means to manifest and clarify the Great Way."
Kāśyapa practiced the dhūta austerities and received the robe of the World-Honored One; his *upādhyāya* followed the regulations of Baizhang and ascended the seat of the Tathāgata.
I do not know whether the Kāśyapa of former times and the one at Eagle Peak today are the same or different. The Master said, "The empty space beneath the courtyard shall explain it for you;
there is no need for this mountain monk to speak further. The Seat-holder said, "I have already received the Master’s indication regarding their sameness or difference."

[The Master] said, "To demonstrate: how is the matter of the single-lineage transmission of the fundamental principle? After a long silence, the Master said, "I am glad that the assembly has all already understood.
A member of the assembly said, "The affairs of thirty years ago were different; after thousands of white [days], the ancestral lamp is new. The Master descended from his seat.

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The Buddhas constantly preach the Dharma at all times; there is no need for deliberation or conjecture as to what dharma it is. Heaven and earth are dark blue and yellow; the universe is vast and ancient.
It matters not whether one penetrates the source or masters the teachings; it is simply a matter of directly taking responsibility. What is it that you take responsibility for?"
Clouds rise and bring forth rain; dew solidifies into frost. A dragon does not dwell in stagnant water; how could a fierce tiger roam by the roadside?

If you can penetrate these pivotal points, what need is there to aspire to go to the Western Land? Without asking whether one is a former Buddha or a later patriarch, the nostrils alike radiate light.
How do they radiate light? Their transformation covers the grasses and trees, reaching out to benefit all quarters. Śākyamuni did not...
Willingly revealing what was hidden: Bodhidharma concealed it for nine years; Mount Emei did not spare his verbal karma and, with a single stroke, proclaimed it for the sake of the assembly.
But tell me, how was it proclaimed? He brandished his staff once and said: "Do not speak of others' shortcomings;
do not rely on your own strengths. Then he descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall:
An old man with blind eyes and a deaf, hard-of-hearing sister-in-law have both lost their senses of form and sound—just as they should.
Furthermore, there is a handless man boxing and a tongueless man discoursing on the Way. Four of them discuss long and short together, while one among them laughs himself right over. And so it is.
The Master laughed and said, "What is there to laugh at? How extraordinary! Puhua has performed a somersault; he truly does not disgrace the legacy of the Golden-Colored Dhūta.
He then ascended the hall for the discourse.
Last night the Empty King transmitted a message: he does not permit monks to travel to sacred sites. Let thorns grow along the path of awakening;
let the profound gate be opened or closed as it pleases. Even so, one must nevertheless accord with the intent of the Empty King.
After a long silence, he said: "In front of the gate the bamboo baskets remain green; behind the hall the pines continue their resonant song. The jade cups and silver lamps..."
The light is restored and bright; from the golden incense burner, precious seals rise in misty clouds. Yet there is a further, true significance:
the plum blossom alone claims the spring of the year. [Descend from the seat.]
Ascending the hall, he held up one point: Buddhas and Patriarchs are all seized by it. Letting down one point: Sages and Worthies are all bound by it.
The revolving wheel flies up to the celestial court; the earthen ox sleeps at the corner of the earth. Not only do the nine realms receive its grace, but the four modes of birth as well.
To experience this bliss, there are only the eight great Vajras with glaring eyes and furrowed brows, brandishing their weapons crosswise and upside down. Why?
Because it is not permitted for sentient beings to make haphazard sketches of them.
Ascending the hall: "The green mountains are green; there is no mountain that does not harbor clouds. The green waters are green; there is no water that does not give rise to trees.
Only the mind of the patch-robed monk is straight and without crookedness. With a single stroke of his ruler, he descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall:
True sons of the dragons and elephants sometimes cannot lift up what they have let go, and sometimes cannot let go of what they have lifted up.
They do not play with the head of a dead snake; they wish to stroke the tail of a living tiger. Sometimes they mount the back of a golden-haired lion, whereupon it is natural—
A pure breeze rises from beneath your feet. Is it so? Ehi! The waters do not dry up, and the fish are at ease;
the mountains are green and secluded, and the birds are serene. Take care.

Ascending the hall on the Winter Solstice: when the solstice arrives, the occasion is truly extraordinary. The sea wind blows down the coral branches; the Dragon Kings startle awake and return to the realm of emptiness;
the River Lords and all the deities lose their majesty. Such matters should be known by oneself. A monk asked, "What is the use of knowing? [The Master said: "If you know, what would you do with it?"
The Master said, "Hold the staff for this old monk. The monk said, "It would be even better if one did not know such things. The Master asked, "Why?
The monk replied, "A monk does not seek mere leisure; on the contrary, he becomes a man of sorrow. The Master then struck him.
Ascending the hall, the Iron Arhat encounters the Crimson-Sounding Fire-Vajra. The two houses vie in spirit, contending with stubborn strength.
With deluded feelings unresolved, he questions the Empty King. The King says: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent. Does the assembly of wise ones understand this meaning? No.
Nevertheless, listen once more to this verse: The courtyard of this wild monk does not follow worldly sentiments; How could he ever allow the white clouds to linger here?
Heaven and earth do not obscure true cause and effect; In this certainty, there is no concern for those on the other shore. *Chan.* (Investigate!)

Ascending the hall, the Head Seat requested, saying: "Having eaten the Nanyue ox-head rice to satiety, one sings songs atop a solitary peak; having drunk the Caoshan wine to intoxication, one sleeps soundly at the crossroads of the marketplace.
For such as these, who blur the distinction between the holy and the mundane, you must fully raise up the Ultimate Teaching. We beg the Master [to speak]."

[Zhengji] asked: "The Master said: 'A man without a nose-tip has no home in the great earth. One with the Way-mind dwells in peace wherever they are. At all times, they are free and expansive; this has its own source.
Utterly forgetting conditions, each is beyond clear definition. As for what has come above, there is no need to question it further—the truth is already known beforehand.
As for what follows below, do not try to explain it away—it is certainly already verified. Relying on the *zhililu* (monk’s staff)..."

His staff probes the ocean and reaches toward the heavens; even when Śakra and the Dragon Kings hear of him, they tremble with fear. Relying on but a single bowl and three robes, he braves winter and defies summer.

Yet when benevolent rulers and high ministers behold him, they incline their hearts in devotion. This is not for the sake of seeking fame or treading upon heights; rather, it is simply because the Dharma compels him to be thus.
May the great assembly each maintain this resolve and follow in the footsteps of the predecessors. As Fengxue said of Baizhang: [and so forth].
Ding: At Mount Yaoshan, [Nanyue Huairang] lived in a cattle pen; at Mount Weishan, [Daowu Yuanzuo] gathered acorns and chestnuts for food;
and at Daming, [Changqing Daoming] constantly gathered lotus leaves for clothing. Lenzan lacked the skill to wipe away his tears, while Baizhang demonstrated the precept of neither acting nor eating.
Beyond these, those who achieved true inquiry and genuine awakening are too numerous to list; each was fully resolved, soaring like the great Peng bird.
Ten thousand *li* cover the earth and screen the heavens; like a lion cub, its majesty shakes the ten directions, startling the multitudes and terrifying the crowds.
It is said that "it is man who can propagate the Way, not the Way that propagates man. You gentlemen should each take this to heart.
Ascending the hall: Delusion gives rise to stillness and turmoil; awakening is without preference for good or evil. But what of it after awakening?
Whether saint or ordinary person is difficult to grasp—a hairless tiger with horns upon its head. Turning over, one intends to debate with the King of Emptiness; a fine steed pursues.
The wind cannot catch up. Is it? Is it not? Is it neither is nor is not? Return! Come back! Going and returning, coming and going. It was not the head monk who let out a laugh;
a million beings among gods and men were all ignorant of it. Having stood for a long time, take care.

Ascending the hall, the Dharma drum sounds three times and the assembly gathers like clouds. Look, look! The crimson sun rises above the balustrade; a pure breeze penetrates the armpits and auspicious clouds arise.
That matter is clear and not hidden—do you all understand? The assembly remains silent. The Master said: "As for this..."

"Ma! Is it that the assembly deceives this mountain monk, or does this mountain monk deceive the assembly? If you say that this mountain monk deceives the assembly, the Great Being Weituo will not be pleased.
Ultimately, how is it so? A precious gem may be used to divide a city, yet one still consents;
one must know the Knower before one can truly accept it. [He descends from his seat.]
Ascending the hall to strike the bell and beat the drum, entering the room and mounting the dais—these are the regulations of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and the standards of the monastic groves.

If you have not yet clarified the "three eights and nine," do not be confused or alarmed. Incense burns in the burner, silver lamps shine upon the altar; within this single room, monks and laypeople alike, like clouds and water, gather together.

Two lines: The night is still and the clouds have gathered; heaven and earth are bright. A cold wind whistles through, piercing the heart with coolness. There is no transmitted teaching outside the Western Arrival;

it is exceedingly clear, so there is no need for further detail. Whether you understand or not: the cypress in front of the courtyard bears fruit that never withers; the rice of Luling rots and sprouts as seedlings.
Old Śākyamuni opens the door; the Great Being Vimalakīrti rises from his bed. Each and every one is distinct.
He spoke clearly, raising the matter once more. The assembly prostrated and each returned to the hall. Wielding his staff, he said: "Accept it directly.

Ascending the hall, he wielded the staff once and said: "The matters within the School of the Patriarchs are difficult to express in words; how can the gateway of the Great Way tolerate conceptualization?"

Consider this: when he casually utters a single phrase, it is like the blade of the Tai-ya sword drawn from its scabbard; whoever encounters it perishes before a moment passes. It is like a "poison-painted" drum struck by a mallet;
whoever hears it dies before their heels even touch the ground. As the saying goes: "The wondrous peak is so steep that wild beasts find no place to hide;
the precious tree’s crystalline radiance is such that numinous birds cannot alight upon it. Its function is simply to drive the golden-haired lion back to his wild lair.
He pursued Tie'e directly into the deep mountains, sweeping away the *chānqīng* (comets/omens of rebellion) across the world and brushing aside the filth and debris of the age.
He rescued those fallen into pits and ditches, and lifted up those lost in delusion or trapped within their stagnant shells; such was his merit.
He caused the Dharma-realm, the world-realm, and the space-realm to be perceived as a single body, and enabled the convergence of all phenomena—the paths of Buddhas, humans, and hell-beings—into one.
Although it is thus, it is still not yet the matter of the upward direction. You must know that there is yet another phrase that transcends the standard and lies outside of measure.
How would you say it? Alas! When the true command is not yet carried out, the head is struck off first; once the great function is unleashed, even sages and worthies feel sorrow.
I have stood for a long time; take care.
Ascending the hall, at times I tell you that which the Buddhas cannot speak; at times I tell you that which sentient beings cannot awaken to.
That which sentient beings can awaken to is what the Buddhas cannot speak; that which the Buddhas can speak is what sentient beings cannot awaken to.
If one does not attain awakening, it is impossible. Should one awaken, they will walk upon the crowns of all Buddhas;

even the sages of a thousand generations will fold their hands in reverence, let alone the hosts of celestial Māras, who will not submit of their own accord. Is there, then, anyone who has attained awakening? Heh!
One joyfully listens to the lingering songs of woodcutters, yet one fears hearing the elegant strains of the "Snow Song."
On the Hall, Guo Feng has a single phrase. It is not the transmission of the Buddhas, nor is it the Zen of the Patriarchs. It does not permit people to speculate or deliberate;
it values only those with the karmic affinity who can directly comprehend it. Do you understand? That which is atop one’s head is ultimately not heaven. [The feet...]
Those who tread upon it ultimately find it is not earth. Having penetrated this heavy barrier, there is yet another true message. The Sixth Patriarch did not understand the Chan of the South;
Bodhidharma did not understand the meaning of his coming from the West. *Chan*.
A small-scale sermon (xiaochan) is certainly not empty, like a person grasping at the wind; it is certainly empty, like a bird caught in a cage. Though empty, it is not empty;
the Buddha does not dwell within it. The Buddha is fundamentally non-existent—who is there to be present or absent? A lamp-pillar gives birth to a child who knows how to conduct business.
The seller originally had not a single coin; the buyer would not accept even a single piece. Only the spring breeze knows it for itself;
at the tips of the hundred grasses, it can manifest all manner of wonders. [Descend from the seat.]

Small Assembly: Peach blossoms are red, plum blossoms are white; the mountains and rivers are narrow. The black rooster stands upright, its body not black. The Tamer of Men has not yet realized his own mind.
To say that form is emptiness and emptiness is form—how do you speak the single phrase that does not fall into form or emptiness? (After a long silence)
It is said: "The yang emerges and the yin returns; spirits appear and ghosts vanish. These are not merely a pack of wild foxes; each and every one of them stands as a Buddha from the very ground up.
If you seek out those from antiquity until the present day, they are all nothing but people filling pits and digging burrows. Be careful! Be careful!
A small instruction for those who study the Way: if your eye of the Path has not yet been clarified, you must simply contemplate a *huatou* (critical phrase).

You must establish a firm and resolute will, like a single person facing ten thousand enemies; only by remaining composed and striking out with full intent can you prevail. Be thus diligent, moment by moment.
Indeed. What does it matter what color it is, or what sound it makes? It matters not whether it is an enemy or a kinsman;
it matters not whether it is a Buddha or an ordinary person. It is not that we disregard them; rather, there is a mortal adversary present. To protect life, one must kill;
only when all are killed does one find peace. Although this is so, it is the most effortless way: there is no need to recite sutras, nor is there any need to prostrate before the Buddha.
There is no need for sitting meditation, no need for traveling on pilgrimage; no need to study texts, no need to seek explanations;
no need to evaluate public cases (gong'an), no need to receive the precepts; no need for ascetic practices, no need for quietude.
At all times and in all places, one sees only that the "head-word" (huatou) is clear; one sees nothing else. Suddenly, in a single moment, there is a flash of realization, as if—
The sun rises in the sky, pervading the ten directions; the entire earth is this very *huatou*.
This is what is called "breaking through the Great San Pass and entering directly into the gate of liberation. Only at such a juncture is one truly empowered. Therefore it is said:

"The place where one gains power is precisely the place where effort is spared. It is only upon reaching this state that one has the capacity for discourse and can truly discern people; this is the "feeling pole" (*tantun*).
It is in your hands. You attain great freedom and are no longer confined by cages.

You may contemplate the *zong* (the essence of the school), you may contemplate the *jiao* (the teachings), you may travel to distant lands, you may mingle with the multitude, or you may dwell in solitude. Therefore it is said: "I am the Dharma King; I am sovereign over the Dharma.
All is one, and one is all. There is no second person. If this matter does not arise from your own mind...
If you have a single moment of realization, even if you possess insights, they will be like "speaking of food without being satiated.
A true man of great capacity will certainly not stop at mere words and deceive himself. If you do not tread to the very bottom, you will surely be unwilling to rest.

Only when you reach the bottom will you no longer be turned by the conditions of various dharmas; you will naturally possess the capacity for transformation and understanding, taking a step forward wherever a Buddha is present, and [remaining] where there is none.
The Buddha places one move, such that no sage or worthy being can frustrate him. What "handle" could they possibly find?
Heaven and earth, yin and yang, calculations and constraints cannot bind him. As for cause and effect, merit and retribution—what can they do?

Even if Buddhas and patriarchs were to arrive here, they would have no choice but to swallow their voices and endure their breath; how much more so for others? This is because he has attained the Great Totality.
This is the *Dhāraṇī-rāja-samādhi*. You must cherish and respect it deeply.
To the assembly:
this matter has nothing else to it; it simply requires that each person understand how to be cautious from the very beginning, so as not to allow the thoughts of birth and death to strike.
Chè: Working on the practice within the ghost-cave of Black Mountain, those who gain too much fall into congestion;
those who gain nothing at all fall into a void. Wisdom inevitably leads one to the realm of cleverness; forgetting one's effort often leads to self-proclaimed isolation.

This has utterly ruined the practice of closing the door and gazing at the wall, wasting so much salt and vinegar. Had it not been for the severing of the arm to settle the mind, how could one know the path back today?
When asked for his name, Shigede simply folded his hands twice and handed him over. Indeed, within the very midst of gaining strength lies the place where effort is exhausted.
If one were to deliberate through intellectual reasoning, it would make even the Elder Kāśyapa laugh to death.
Look at such a method—what difficulty could there be in attaining Buddhahood? It only requires that people of today cease their madness; do not rely on a state of cessation as the goal.
"Staying at home. Indeed, it is better not to have good things at all. Do not mistake non-action for evasive maneuvering. Descend from the seat.
Having finished the field-clearing, he addressed the assembly:

"The great assembly has exerted their utmost effort to clear the fields for the permanent residence; I, this mountain monk, have exerted my utmost effort to preach Chan for the great assembly. Last night..."
At the third watch, the thunder rumbled; it shattered half the horn of the mud-dragon. Descending from the seat, he addressed the assembly on the eve of the New Year:
"Spring is about to arrive and winter has already returned. I inform you all: take this as a means for self-reflection. At the critical juncture of birth and death, you have not yet struck through."
Chè! Do not let the *huatou* run wild or wander in confusion. This time, you shall receive no method of ease. Vast and boundless, the karmic consciousness has nothing to rely upon.

All the eminent sages of the past and present who have investigated the mystery have turned it back toward the present moment. Turn it back toward the present moment; awakening will then have its time.
To overturn heaven and earth depends on oneself. If you wish to rekindle the flame with Dīpaṃkara, you must first let the fire go out.
It was reduced to flying ashes. Yet, even though it is thus, you should know: how can one speak that single phrase outside the teachings?
The Muni of the Western Heaven has departed; Bodhidharma of the Eastern Land has returned.
When the Master moved next to Bao-fang, after the opening address of the hall and the striking of the mallet had concluded, the Master said:
"Does the assembly understand the primary meaning? If you do not understand it, then for now turn toward the secondary."
He takes this up within the meaning [of the teaching] and lets out a shout, saying: "Do you understand? If one discusses this matter, it values practice and conduct.

It is like a traveler walking a path; when the path ends, he climbs a tree. When he reaches the very top of the tree, he takes another step forward, and then he dwells together with the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
But as for this one step—how does one take it? Heh! The shadow of the cassia tree soars into the void; those with eyes [see it]."
All gaze upon it, except for those who are blind. Hearing this, do not harbor doubts. The spring breeze does not reside upon the flowering branches;
let the Lingfeng Peak do as it pleases, crying out to the cuckoo. Be careful and heedful.
After sitting for a long while on the high seat, he said: "Does the assembly understand? If you understand in this way, you are still somewhat close;

yet if it is not so, then even if you claim 'the Way exists before the eyes,' I dare say you have not yet arrived. To transmit the mind through strings and flutes ultimately results in a persistent obstruction. [He struck] the black lacquer...
The bottom of the bucket reflects appearances and discriminates colors; upon the unperforated iron hammer, one pursues scent and seeks sound.
To ask further, "Which one is it? is to kill people with gasping breath. Precious timber for rafters and beams on a rocky cliff is but a vain hope for the carpenter;

a dragon-steed from a sea island, a vessel for the state, is but empty chanting by generals. What was accomplished by facing the wall for nine years? Only when the mind cannot be found does one find peace.
"Mind. He spoke again, saying, "Great assembly, thirty years from now, do not say that Baofang was without reason for his critiques of the ancients and the present.

If one says "it does not exist," from whom did the forty-seven patriarchs of India and the twenty-three ancestors of this land derive their authority? From what cause did the masters of the five schools establish their lineages?

Therefore it is said: when the matter is extremely profound, even ghosts and spirits find it a meal they cannot digest; yet the most obscure phrase is precisely where the Buddhas and Patriarchs reside.
"Claws and fangs. Nevertheless, although it is thus, let those among the assembly who possess the eye of discernment come forward to clarify this with their eloquence.
After a long silence, he said: "At the point where the road ends and the mountains reach their limit, quickly fix your eyes upon it! Then he descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, there is only this. How can it be? It is great yet not large; it is small yet not small. How lofty is the void!
How remote are the ends of heaven! Śākyamuni was not clever; Bodhidharma was full of leaks. Six years in the Snowy Mountains were merely a false reliance.
In the past, he faced the wall for nine years, remaining silent; from generation to generation, this has been handed down from antiquity to the present.
Who can anticipate the opening of the pivot before it moves? Only the Elder Wooden Seat knows how to laugh "he-he."
Ascending the hall:
pulling out the sinews without moving the skin; changing the bones without seeing blood. When the tendons and bones are all at once empty, one wanders about without falling.
The Great Master Bodhidharma understood extinction but did not understand birth; the Elder Śākyamuni understood birth but did not understand extinction.
One must know that arising and ceasing do not interfere with one another; apart from this, it is merely last year’s dried dung.

When ascending the hall, if there were even a single principle, True Suchness and the Ultimate Reality would find no name for it; if there were not even a single principle, the Great Being Samantabhadra...

There is no place to hide oneself. If you say it is both existent and non-existent, you have not avoided being muddled. If you say it is neither existent nor non-existent, this is still merely a vague generality.
But if one sets these aside, how then can one establish a definitive standard? The assembly was silent. The Master said: "Heaven and earth have no private intent;
sages and worthies have no separate mind. Before Bodhidharma came to the Eastern Land, [the truth] was manifest at Mount Nanyue and Tiantai."
[The assembly] is seated. Descend from your seat.
As for the one who ascends the hall before the entire assembly of knowledgeable ones today—this must be decisively established; do not say:
The regulations are lifted in the early morning. Why is this? The white ox in the open field has left no trace; how could it ever be willing to retire all at once?
One must shatter empty space and search with intent; see where it hides its tracks. If you find it, bind it firmly by the nose;
only when you have ridden it back home will you be noble. Entrust this to Nanquan and Guishan: let us all keep watch together.
*Ra li*. When sentient beings hear or see this, all are as such; they shall all go together to the Dragon Flower Assembly. Have you not heard the ancient masters say:
"It is present before the face-gate all day long, exposed and wide open; even if you try to chase it away, it will not go"?

If you can attain such a state, only then will you not have brought shame upon Śākyamuni Buddha’s appearance in the world. As for my saying, "Sit in meditation for a moment"—is there anyone who can? *Ei*. There is an intention.
When the breath moves, it adds to one’s spirit; even in moments that are not inherently elegant, there is elegance. Descend from the seat.
As he approaches death and takes leave of the assembly, he ascends the hall and says:
"This year, there is but this single moment remaining. I ask you all: do you know it or not? That matter has never yet been personally struck."
[This is] essential. You must apply yourself with constant and meticulous effort. All the Buddhas and Patriarchs of the past did so for this very reason.

Formerly, under the guidance of Guizong, a monk shouted loudly at night, saying, "I have attained enlightenment! The next day, Guizong ascended the hall and said, "The monk who had a great awakening last night, come forward and speak.
When the monk stepped forward, he said, "A nun is originally made by a woman. As for Guizong—[the rest follows] like a horse.
Under the Patriarch, there emerged more than eighty virtuous teachers (śāstrakalyāṇamitra); Guizong was one of them.
If this monk had not reached this state with absolute certainty, how could he have been granted approval?
O Assembly, examine this koan from left to right, turning it over and over and looking at it closely: what principle is it? Is there any Buddha-dharma here, or is there not? Is there...?
Even the vehicle of our school does not exist; let us rejoice that there is no further connection. This is the final instruction I, this old monk, bestow today.
The assembly should cherish it with all earnestness.
Small Assembly:
If the mind realized is as empty as space, even fine motes of dust cannot fly there; how much less could the traces of sages or ordinary beings rely upon it?
One who thoroughly understands this empty mind explains the Way of Non-arising; it once caused stones to nod their heads, yet even Universal Eye (Samantabhadra) could not seek it out.

The left is good; the right is good. Walking alone in the Great Way, he is free from affliction. For nearly fifty years he has preached the Dharma, yet among it all, he has forgotten not a single word.
Life after life, birth after birth, within the Dharma-realm, he humbles his dignity to accommodate the lowly and upholds those who are inverted.
Again, he raises his whisk and says: "Look! Look! You must have the head straight and the tail straight before you can succeed."
Small Assembly:

If the mind possesses even a single dharma, it will find no peace wherever it dwells. If the mind lacks even a single dharma, one cannot avoid being muddled and superficial. When the mind clings to neither existence nor non-existence, what is its ultimate state?
The mountains and rivers obstruct the eyes, yet the emotional mind does not flicker; the objective world resides within the chest, yet consciousness has not yet dried up.
Therefore, it is not permitted to act thus; it is not permitted not to act thus; it is not permitted to act both thus and not thus.
Only by penetrating beyond these three propositions will you naturally be no different from the Buddha. You may move crosswise, you may move straight ahead—there is nothing that can obstruct you.
You fear neither death nor life; how could you fail to avoid a clash of blades? For you possess a path that pierces through the heavens.
The Path. When traveling upon the bird-path, where can one seek its traces? Like an illusory person, it cannot be grasped;
even Buddhas and Patriarchs are helpless against it, let alone heaven and hell. O Great Assembly, you must believe that this principle exists.

"If one does not fall into the categories of sage or ordinary person, how would you express this in a single phrase? After a long silence, he said: "The Great Garuda spreads its wings and the Flying Dragon trembles;
the Lion roars repeatedly and the Great Elephant is startled."
Small Assembly:
When not a single thought arises, Buddhas and sentient beings have no dualistic appearance. Let not the three minds stir; the five houses and hundred schools are all but solitary luminosity.
In the ten directions and three periods of time, who is at peace? Within the six realms and four modes of birth, what can be established? There is nothing to be realized; yet, one realizes it.
One fundamentally realizes one's own mind; clarity is clarity without an object of clarity. When there is clarity, it is simply the clarity of the original nature.

The Tripitaka does not discuss separate matters, and how could the Five Houses expound another vehicle? Because the principle of nature has not been thoroughly penetrated, ten thousand kinds of discrepancies arise. If the ground of the mind is clear, [all distinctions vanish].
He thoroughly harmonized the skeletal remains of a hundred schools; ascending the profound path, he spread the net of meaning. The pivot of the lock was shattered, and the mass of doubt was broken.

No longer lingering in phrases or following words, he let the *tathāgata-puṣpa* (Dharma-flowers) bloom across the fields at will. He ultimately ceased his counting of characters and strokes, allowing the *palm-leaf* scriptures to scatter as far as the heavens.
For what reason did he undergo six years of ascetic practice? It was solely for the sake of the "Evolving Head" (*Añjanāvat*). For nine years, he faced... [the mirror].
This wall has accomplished a great matter by exclusively attracting those who have fled. Viewed with the correct eye, it is truly like a dream. There is only the One Truth, and all is true;
the use of staffs and shouts is merely a vain exertion. All phenomena are but a single phenomenon; killing and enlivening are but a wrongful application of practice.

A thousand sages cannot do anything about it; it is simply that from the beginning there is nothing at all. That all quarters exert their utmost efforts to take refuge and look up to it is entirely because it is, in its very essence, completely empty.
Let the five ranks be arranged as they may; if one seeks its traces, they are utterly unobtainable.

When the three mysteries are opened, even if one seeks its influence or shadow, it is ultimately difficult to know. Even a hundred thousand Mañjuśrīs could not, through their supernatural powers, surpass a single Nāga.
Puhua’s spiritual traces startled the great earth. How could they compare to the wild fox’s ability to manifest transformations?
Even if one were able to escape Huangbo’s snare, one would still be made to vomit in indignation before Nanquan.
When scrutinized, all those under the three thousand gates and the millions of devas and humans have been struck with the staff. But tell me, where does the fault lie? *Ai!* It is simply because...
To exist now is not to have escaped non-existence in the past.

In this informal discourse, walking does not traverse the direct path, and sitting does not involve the meditation seat. Released, there is no trace; gathered, there is no mark. For the most part, this is the universal principle.
A unique extraction: Raising the fist and brandishing the sword transcends the ordinary; in the distinct gateways there are no fixed rules.
Let it all follow the path of wisdom without mutual obstruction.
Small Session (Xiaocan).

In the Buddha-dharma, what is valued regarding both dharma and non-dharma is awakening and reaching. In the path of the Patriarchs, where there is neither path nor non-path, one must personally arrive.

To awaken is to resolve the right and wrong of sage and ordinary; to arrive is to sever the karmic retribution of humans and devas. Whether one awakens or not, the certainty of non-arising will spontaneously manifest in a single thought-moment.
Once it has manifested, a thousand lamps share a single light; there is no need to further deliberate upon arising and ceasing. Whether one arrives or not, [the truth is] one...
Contemplate with pure sincerity and act with true integrity. When the time comes for the conditions and capacities to ripen, even empty space will surely fall down.

What need is there to discuss Buddhas and Patriarchs? What need is there to talk of the Way of the Dharma? Throughout the ten directions and the entire dharma-realm, all traces of movement are severed; where can one seek mirage-water or flowers in the sky?
Small Assembly:
You who have gathered here for this Dharma assembly should take the Dharma as your primary concern. If you do not attain the Dharma, what benefit is there in your practice?
Why is this? This Dharma is none other than your own mind. As the ancients said: "The mind itself is Buddha; the mind itself is the Dharma. The Dharma...
The Buddha is non-dual; the Jewel of the Sangha is likewise so. Thus it is said: "All phenomena arise from the mind. Do you still recognize this mind?

It is that very thing which, right now, is vividly present, solitary and luminous, shining brightly throughout heaven and earth. Furthermore, an ancient said: "The dharma of the mind has no form, yet it pervades and fills the ten directions.
This mind, when in the eye, can see the forms of the ten directions; when in the ear, it can hear the sounds of the ten directions. It is like...

These six gates are all capable of discernment and awareness; you must examine and awaken to this yourself. If you do not recognize this mind, even if you cultivate the ten wholesome deeds, it is not liberation;
even if you attain great meditative concentration, it is not the ultimate; even if you possess eloquence and wisdom, you will only achieve dry wisdom and remain unable to escape saṃsāra.
Do not say that merely by emptying the five aggregates, one can cross over all suffering and calamity.

If one does not know that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are fundamentally empty, how could suffering and affliction exist? Does the Sūtra not say: "Form is not different from emptiness; emptiness is not different from form.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this"? Emptiness is the mind; form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also the mind.
Therefore, whatever forms are perceived are all perceptions of the mind. As the Sūtra says: "All things in the world..."
All things are, in their entirety, the wondrously luminous essence of Bodhi. When this mind is once awakened to, there is no form, no sensation, perception, mental formation, or consciousness;
no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; and even no wisdom and no attainment. One is all, and all is one.
If you can be thus, why worry about not reaching completion? If you do not awaken, it is simply because within the phenomena of the mind...
Examine this by looking through the entirety of the ten directions. When you suddenly penetrate it, your radiance will surpass the sun and moon, and you will encompass heaven and earth;
only then is it the point of entry. You may then be certain that you have a share in the discourse, and naturally you will not be bound by any matters of existence or non-existence. Be careful!
Small Assembly:
Last night, thunder crashed and lightning flashed, shattering the void; my brain was split open in bitter resentment as I appealed to Vairocana, yet he could not provide a fair judgment.
Does anyone among the assembly know how to clear his name for him? A monk said, "It all depends on the Master. The Master [laughed].
It is said: "Let us give him a slap.

On the occasion of the small assembly (xiaochan) at the end of the year, it is the thirtieth night; one should know the point of final reckoning. Clouds follow the dragon; wind follows the tiger. Nine times nine is eighty-one.
One. Five times five is twenty-five. The four-seven schools of the Western Heaven; the two-three patriarchs of the Eastern Land.
If the sweet melon is sweet all the way to its stem, the bitter gourd is bitter down to its roots. Zhaozhou and Huangbo do not fall within these numbers. *Chan*.
Small Assembly: I recall years past when I reached the age of forty; Plowing rice seedlings in the fields, I knew not their source. Now, fortunately, I have attained the longevity of seventy;
As before, I go into the fields to drive the oxen. Planting grain to earn one’s meal is an ancient custom; I wonder, who among you can share in this?
"Make a companion. If there were one, he would have come here to carry my hoe and hold my rain-hat for me.
After a long silence, he said, "It is not so. As before, the Old Monk must handle it himself. For forty or fifty years I have beaten these two pieces of skin;
now, it is utterly impossible to find even a single person to carry the hoe and hold the hat. Take care."

In this informal discourse, I do not tread upon the upright weeds, nor do I grasp at the horizontal ones. Beyond the four modes of deportment, all subtle entanglements are severed. The Daoist does not study the Way; why? Because he is but a piece of wood.
The Chan practitioner does not practice Chan; for what reason? Because he is but a brick or a tile. Had it not been for Bodhidharma coming here, how could this have been so?

Know that the "separate transmission outside the teachings" does not mean that plucking a reed to cross the river was his original intent; sitting facing a wall for nine years was merely an expedient means.
Zen practitioners should truly exert yourselves in this regard. Small Assembly Sermon.
A single boat rides upon the great sea; the great sea encompasses all the tides. When red dust covers the earth, how can it be dispelled?

When white waves surge to the heavens, how can they be extinguished? If there be among the assembly anyone who can seize the clouds and leap over the waves, snatch the drums and race for the banners—please, try to exert your strength and see!
Otherwise, the *utpala* flower will not be scattered in disorder.
A Small Sermon on the Hour of Death:

Human life involves receiving [karmic results] rather than repaying them. Do not be panicked by old age, sickness, and death. Break through with the Dharma-patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and the karmic consciousness will naturally vanish.
In an instant, the clouds clear and the eternal light shines forth; Buddhas and Patriarchs all abide within this very site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). Therefore it is said:
I now abide in the light of eternal quiescence and extinction, which is named Great Nirvāṇa.

Even if Buddhas and patriarchs were to skillfully reveal various profound and subtle gateways, employing the seven directions and eight expedients to guide and attract all capacities, it would all ultimately not transcend this light of great quiescent extinction.
Take heed.
Those who study the Buddha-way must, above all, not remain on the stage of learning; they must proceed until they reach the ground of the Buddhas and Patriarchs before they have attained it.
Therefore, although Sudhana visited over a hundred cities, he simply asked, "I have previously resolved to attain Bodhicitta;

how should I be instructed to study the path of a Bodhisattva? This is like saying that there is not a single dharma that can be named as Bodhicitta—the realization attained by the successive patriarchs above—how could there be even the slightest dharma to be obtained?
Thus, a monk asked Jiufeng Qian: "The patriarchs transmit it from one to another."
"What further matter was transmitted? The Master said, "Śākyamuni was stingy; Kāśyapa was wealthy. The monk asked, "What is Śākyamuni’s stinginess?
The Master said, "He had nothing to give to others. The monk asked, "What is Kāśyapa’s wealth? The Master said, "The Lord Mengchang within the borders of the kingdom.
The monk asked, "Ultimately, what was the matter that was transmitted? The Master said, "An old man of a hundred years dividing his night lamp."
Look closely: there are those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa). Even so, it is only by practicing that one comes to know such a thing exists.
Yet, among those who practice but do not study, nine out of ten arrive; among those who study but do not practice, not even one in ten arrives.
When both study and practice are complete, ten out of ten cultivate and ten out of ten arrive. Thus, Śākyamuni practiced austerities for six years, and Bodhidharma faced the wall for nine years.
Mazu did not open his mouth for twenty years; Zhaozhou was still traveling on foot at the age of eighty;
Kefu spent his entire life wearing paper robes; Xuantai lived his whole life in cotton patchwork robes; Zhang Jiucheng contemplated the "pine tree"; and Lü Chunfu held up Zhaozhou’s “no.
Those who have attained this essential meaning throughout the ages are beyond the capacity of pen and tongue to fully describe—each and every one of them.
This is practiced in actual conduct. At once, the lacquer bucket is shattered; naturally, everything is in accord with every aspect, and every thing is clear.

That which has been used exhaustively throughout antiquity and the present has now reached your hands. When you wish to use it, it is truly like a poor woman’s *lanca* grass—picked up by the hand as needed.
Do not merely practice; even if you study until you pass through the belly of the Tripitaka, [the essence remains] within the seventeen hundred [cases].
Thus, it is brought forth; yet when the fixed karma arrives, one cannot avoid a scene of great turmoil. One reflects that there is no other thought, only this "A-ya. But what is this fixed karma?
It is precisely the realm of habitual use since beginningless time. Although one knows this fault and exerts all effort to clear it away, it becomes increasingly chaotic.
The power of practice does not endure long; and though one continues to cultivate progress, it still does not...
Know that ignorance and awakening have been fused and rolled into a single mass. If you wish to settle this karmic enemy and disperse them, first, do not try to sweep them away.
Simply take up a "critical phrase" (huatou) regarding the confrontation with birth and death and place it directly before you to resist them.
Then, those idle spirits and wild ghosts within the cavern of deluded thoughts, as well as the goblins, ogres, and the multitudes of Buddhas and demons, will surely scatter.

It cannot be attained through mere proximity. In the past, Pāṇṭaka held a broom for thirty years; his mind of birth and death was shattered, and he realized the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
How could there be one who practices with total exertion and yet fail to have a sudden awakening? Nevertheless, you must by no means speak of it as easy out of license.
For thirty years, this mountain monk has applied himself with real effort in practice, yet I am still unable to avoid being led astray; how much more so for others!
Without applying the effort of death, one cannot achieve realization. Thus, Fenyang said: "The ancients required twenty or thirty years before they finally accomplished it;
how much more so in these times! Whenever I am before others, I do not dare say that this is easy.
Were it not for having applied actual strength to penetrate the very core of the ancients, how would I dare speak such words? This is certainly not mere empty talk or deception.

To deceive others is a crime that can never be considered light. If you all are willing to resolve your minds and apply yourselves to the fundamental practice of Sudhana, taking up the *huatou* (critical phrase) of the various masters, then with a single resolute thought, regardless of distance or time—whether years or months—you will surely attain insight.
It will be like clouds parting to reveal the sun, where the entire earth is bathed in radiance; thus, you will understand that which existed before even the Buddha had set forth.

Everywhere he establishes checkpoints and camps to block the wild foxes; he discriminates between right and wrong, enters the state of equality, and eliminates those who are not yet free from being led astray by the six teachers into the ranks of the worldly fire.
He prevents later generations from being corrupted and defiling the former sages. A true lion cub turns at a single nudge;
he makes a definitive resolution regarding spiritual lineage. Unless one possesses the seal of the special transmission from Kāśyapa, even if one were...

His feet tread upon lotus flowers; his head is shaded by a jeweled canopy. His eloquence flows like a cascading river as he traverses the universe. With a single realization, he speaks forth directly before one's face. Why is this?

It is simply because one must select a means capable of stabilizing heaven and earth, possessing a heart free from dross or impurity, to uphold and revitalize the ancestral wind and serve as an eye for the future.
The Buddha-dharma may not be encountered in a thousand lifetimes; the Way of the Patriarchs endures for ten thousand generations.
Hard to encounter! Fortunately, I have met this by a singular karmic affinity, as if having obtained an unperforated iron hammer. For many years, my body and mind have been mired in confusion;

suddenly, as I was passing beneath a great mountain, it was as if I had obtained a supreme treasure. My body and mind leaped with joy, and even until this present time, its utility remains inexhaustible.
Only now do I realize that the thousand sages have transmitted the bottomless bowl together, which shall remain perpetually fragrant through birth after birth and age after age.
I humbly hope that you will cherish and value this with a sincere mind in the future.

Regarding the ancient precedent concerning Xuefeng Yicun’s response to a monk’s question: "What is one who practices the path of cultivating goodness? The Master replied, "Carrying a cangue and wearing shackles. As it is said:
"What is one who practices evil? The Master said, "One who cultivates meditation and enters samādhi. [The student] said, "My faculties are shallow; I beg the Master for a direct pointing.
The Master said, "If you ask me about evil, evil does not follow from good. If you ask me about good, good does not follow from evil. Do you understand? [The student] said, "I do not understand.
The Master said, "An evil person has no thoughts of goodness; a good person has no thoughts of evil. Therefore it is said, 'Good...'"
"Evil is like floating clouds; both lack a place of arising or ceasing. At these words, the monk attained great enlightenment. The Master remarked, "The evil man has no goodness;
the good man has no evil. In an instant, he knew his home beyond words;

suddenly, he did not fall into cause and effect. The monk was greatly enlightened. What did he awaken to? "The lion cub snaps asunder the golden chain. To speak according to reality: [he realized that] the nature of mind is originally free.
To raise this discussion: both [positions] fail to escape error. Ultimately, where does the error lie? A single strand of drifting cloud gathers upon the green peaks;
let it be stirred by wind and thunder, or withdrawn at will.
A non-Buddhist asked the World-Honored One, saying, "I ask neither for words nor for silence. The World-Honored One remained silent for a long while.
The non-Buddhist praised him, saying, "The World-Honored One’s great compassion has cleared away the clouds of my delusion, enabling me to enter [the Way]. He then prostrated himself and departed.

Ānanda said to the Buddha, "By what principle did the non-Buddhists praise [you] and depart? The World-Honored One replied, "It is like a fine horse of the world that moves at the mere sight of the shadow of the whip."
The Master took up the case, saying: "This matter is what is called 'a voice echoing through an empty valley' or 'listening in a vacant hall.
As for the World-Honored One’s long silence and Zhaojue’s bestowing of the staff—were they the same or different?
If you can discern this, then even a non-Buddhist becomes a Buddha; if not, then a Buddha is but a non-Buddhist. Do you understand? The soaring dragon and dancing phoenix are truly strange!"
"Not for the green-eyed foreign monk to look upon.
Mazu said, "Since the period of chaos, thirty years have passed without me lacking salt or sauce.
The Master [Zhaozhou] commented: "Mazu spoke thus; in my case, it is not so. Since the period of chaos..."
"For thirty years, there has been no salt or sauce. Great assembly, tell me: how far apart are you and Master Ma?
Heh! That was empty talk; this is actual experience."
A monk asked Tong’an, “What is the Teacher of Gods and Humans? An replied, “The horns on his head are not yet complete; the hair on his body has not yet grown. The Master [Zhaozhou] commented:
“Passing through a customs post is easy; traveling across a dangerous mountain pass is difficult. A strategist possesses the ability for foresight; a general...”
Originally relying on the power of majesty and valor, he foreknows treacherous places and avoids treading upon them; he is certain to secure a superior position and ascend it loftily.
Without the need for bloody combat, success is achieved, and the suffering of the soldiers and civilians is well preserved—this proceeds from divine strategy and subtle calculation.

In the end, it was all for nothing. Do you wish to understand the meaning of Tong’an? Suddenly he pulls out a flint capable of igniting a vast plain, startling the spirits dwelling in their nests and caves.
Verse on the Ancient Case:
The World-Honored One Holds Up a Flower.
A precious tripod weighing a thousand *jin* floats upon the vast ocean; a cubit-long hair from a tortoise binds the Great Void. It was not for the sake of Kāśyapa’s smile.
He left the world. How could he possibly have dared to mock a hundred thousand people?
When the World-Honored One saw two men carrying a pig past, he thought:
"A gentleman completes the beauty of another's work. Though there was no wind on level ground, waves arose. Nevertheless, this had nothing to do with the assembly; it was not yet finished.
Beyond the reach of sight, hearing, thought, or deliberation:

when Aṅgulimāla held his almsbowl, sentient beings were mostly entangled by the conditions of the aggregates; yet upon encountering this profound sound, they immediately resolved their grudges, suddenly and utterly transcending into emptiness.
Beyond the kalpas. This was because he had not paid the toll at the end of the road.
While Devadatta was in hell, it was as pleasant as the Third Dhyāna Heaven;
the World-Honored One did not recognize good from evil, and Devadatta did not know life from death, so he suddenly and willfully splashed raw excrement upon him.
This causes all under heaven to ask, "How is it? It is much like standing by a river and crying out for thirst. Heh!
The claws and fangs of the Dharma cave—its majestic power cannot be suppressed. Master Ma’s salt and sauce.
Probing with the staff and shadowing the grass to inquire into the origins—this place ultimately cannot serve as a true response.
For thirty years, this has been the matter of daily tea and rice; how could it ever be gathered up like a precious jewel?
Nanquan’s Beheading of the Cat:
Nanquan is a creature of strange antics; Zhaozhou aids in the evil. This brings trouble upon later generations, who are dragged along by ropes and cords.
Only the cat has ascended high to the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Danxia burned the wooden Buddha;
Danxia did not have kind intentions. He caused people to suffer calamity alive and well. Today, there is no better way to repay his kindness than this:
having lost one's money and incurred guilt, how could one possibly accept it?
Nanquan’s white ox—
whether it knows or does not know— causes the monks of the world to run about in confusion. Even if one were the eight-armed Nala,
touching its nostrils would cause them to lose their mouths.
A monk asked Zhaozhou, “What is the path that is never mistaken? Zhaozhou replied, “To clarify the mind and see one’s nature is the path that is never mistaken.
With a mouth but no heart, this old master—sometimes correct, sometimes wrong.
Though you may possess a thousand skills and wits, in both ancient and modern times, he remains the fatherless son.

The old woman of Mount Tai secretly harbors the colors of spring and openly reveals the radiance of autumn. Though one has eyes, they cannot discern her; though one possesses wisdom, it is difficult to fathom her.
Having reached home, she does not travel the long road to Chang’an; let the wind, flowers, snow, and moon rise as they will.
Severing the true qi-pulse of empty space, sweeping away the orthodox arrangements of sages and worthies— one must know the meaning of the single transmission outside the teachings,
which uproots the common person from their views and hearing.
The abbot held up his fist.
This was Zhaozhou’s fundamental skill. Those who distinguish between superior and inferior are fools; in killing or giving life, he never had any deliberate intent.
There is no need for what is acceptable or unacceptable.
Zhaozhou’s “drinking tea” is a masterful display of killing and enlivening; existence and non-existence are but a single cup of tea.
If one encounters such a guest from Xiantuo, one must ultimately follow them rather than comply with them.
The Seamless Stūpa of Nanyang: When asked, the response is without beginning;
the same applies to what is raised. The golden crow truly does not dwell at the edge of the sky; innate knowledge naturally possesses the divine eye.

Yunmen’s “dry shit-stick”:
a matter of contraction without extension, truly clumsy. It makes it difficult for people to distinguish between hatred and love; how many can see clearly right here and now?
A radish from Zhenzhou has been driven even deeper with a wedge.

Dongshan’s “Three *jin* of Hemp. How many people has it bound and killed? Failing to understand the meaning of the Patriarch, they remain with minds frozen and unmoving.
“Three *jin* of hemp”—what is this? If you attempt to deliberate upon it, there will be no fruit.
The ancient mirror has not yet been polished;
a bundle of withered thatch serves as precious wood. As the smoke rises and fills the Dharma-realm, those who encounter this condition by chance are bathed in its fragrance.
Suddenly, it shatters and scatters throughout the vast void.
When Xiangyan struck the bamboo, time came and iron was transformed into gold; how could it have been found through mere, trivial searching?
By striking the bamboo and hearing the sound of the pebble, he attained great enlightenment—how many people has he not deceived and led astray!
At Nan-yuan, the "cracking and pecking" occur simultaneously.
To summon a snake is easy; to send it away is difficult. Once sent away, who knows that it has the power to turn back?

Fengxue asked a monk, "Regarding the saying 'the chick pecks and the mother hen pries open the shell at the same moment,' how did you understand it then?
The monk replied, "At that time, it was as if I were walking within the light of a lamp. Fengxue said, "You have understood."
Awakening does not come from a teacher; it belongs entirely to conditions. When attained, it still costs no travel expenses.
That which causes the earth to turn and heaven to revolve is the golden sun descending upon the azure river.
Fengxue’s single speck of dust:

Chan Master Qingyuan Xin ascended the hall and said: "Thirty years ago, before I had studied Chan, when I saw mountains, they were mountains;
when I saw water, it was water. Later, after I had personally encountered a teacher and attained a point of entry, when I saw mountains, they were not mountains;

Dizang plants the field;
who among men does not love virtuous descendants? Yet alas, even if they are not virtuous, it is all in vain. The family treasure has already been fully entrusted;

General Verse on the Five Schools:
The School of Guiyang. Reflecting inwardly upon the numinous flame reveals its wondrous inexhaustibility; phenomena and principle are non-dual, penetrating the profound essence.
Bestowing and revoking flow like a continuous stream, all held within the grasp of one’s own hand.
Linji School: The subtle mystery of the seal struck by the staff; three fists and one palm establish the family enterprise, its consequences reaching descendants beyond measure.

The Recorded Sayings of Master Wuming Shouchang, Volume Three:

Question: The World-Honored One opened the hall for forty-nine years and delivered over three hundred assemblies of discourses.

Question: Mañjuśrī is the teacher of the seven Buddhas; why was he unable to emerge from the woman’s samādhi? Wangming is a practitioner of the first bhūmi;

The Master exclaimed, "This wild fox spirit! Drive it out at three feet!

With clanging sounds and playful songs of joy, It keeps people awake all night long.
Question: Why was it that Sudhana could not find the Bhikṣu Meghashiri for seven days when he went to the peak of Mount Sumeru, yet they met on a different peak afterward?
The Master raised a ruler and said: "This is the head of all peaks; I invite Sudhana to come and meet me here."
The verse says: Within every atom, the jeweled king’s lands appear everywhere; how could they possibly meet as one departs for another peak?
Only the wildcat is truly ancient and strange; leaping from the Dharma Hall, it ascends to the highest heavens.
Question: "The First Patriarch sat facing the wall for nine years to directly address those of the highest capacity. I wonder, did he still apply effort?
The Master said: "This useless fellow! What 'effort' could you possibly speak of regarding him?"
The verse says: Unfamiliar with both worldly and world-transcending dharmas, he has come to this land to blabber and prattle.
Though humans, devas, ordinary beings, and sages alike despise him, he has instead gained a pure reputation that enters the charts of the ancestral patriarchs.

Question: When the Second Patriarch preached the Dharma, heavenly flowers fell in profusion and golden lotuses sprang from the earth. Why then did he stand in the snow to seek Bodhidharma’s peace of mind?
The Master said: "This old fellow had a certain intent. He did not know how to use gold to purchase gold; instead, he knew how to use dust to remove dust."
The Verse says: The Tripitaka scriptures fill the shelves of his chest; Heaven and earth alike marvel at this wonder!
If one knows what is not, one severs the arm to seek the Dharma of the Mind; Who would have thought that even this "stupidity" is itself "stupid"?
Question: Shenxiu served as the Master of Instruction under the Fifth Patriarch; for what reason were the robe and bowl bestowed upon the Layman Lu?
The Master said: "How could the Master Lu have ever received the robe and bowl? Do not slander him."
The verse says: An elder loves an elder; a single ingot of gold is returned for a single ingot of gold. One who possesses the eye of wisdom must ultimately recognize the true color;
how could one possibly mistake the balance point on the scale?
A question was asked: "Before Ox-head had seen the Fourth Patriarch, he moved the hundred birds to offer him flowers; why was it that after seeing him, this ceased?
The Master said: "Alas! You pitiable fellow, your eyes have been changed by others. From now on, you shall no longer be able to see spirits or ghosts."
The verse says: How can the glory and splendor of a single lifetime be boasted of? A thousand pieces of gold cannot buy a man of the wilds.
His gate and courtyard are steep and inaccessible, difficult for others to approach; how could birds and beasts ever present him with flowers again?
Question: An ancient said, "Form and sound are the lethal poison of non-arising; sensation, perception, and so forth, even up to consciousness, are the pits and traps for humanity.
Why, then, do you say that one enters nirvana without severing afflictions?
The Master said, "Eh! A snake’s head and a ghost’s brain. The verse says:
By chance entering the Zen garden, one meets a master craftsman; A newly fashioned, fashionable, tattered *kāṣāya*.
Sometimes it wraps around the three thousand worlds; It does not permit people of this age to scatter sand recklessly.
Question: "The green ivy winds its way straight up to the crest of the cold pine; the white clouds drift indistinctly, appearing and disappearing within the vast void.
All phenomena are fundamentally tranquil, yet it is only man who creates turmoil. What, then, is this fundamentally tranquil dharma?"
The Master said: "Walls, tiles, and rubble.
The verse says: "I knew well that in times of national peril, loyal ministers emerge; If one does not encounter hardship and danger, one does not see the true person.
Once you have reached the gate within Nanyang, Why need you further inquire at the frontier checkpoints?"
Question: "When deluded, the three realms exist; upon awakening, the ten directions are empty. I do not yet understand how the central tree-seed can be made to pass through.
The Master said: "In this world of five turbidities, it is truly difficult to seek it out."
The Verse says: The Buddha performed difficult deeds amidst the affairs of a turbid world; Each and every one who hears this should investigate it with earnest application.
Suddenly, one day, the head is struck and shattered; At last, one ceases and departs the pass, no longer seeking the ford.
Question: "Among the myriad phenomena, the body alone is revealed. I do not yet know whether the pillar and the lantern are the same or different.
The Master said: "Eh! You must ask the pillar instead."
The verse says: The winds and moons of the four continents differ; at night they are west, while the sun is east.
This is merely to provide a path for those of this age to understand; Mount Sumeru stands as a barrier between them.

Question: "The Buddha-dharma pervades all places and manifests universally before all sentient beings; why then do some who are deluded remain deluded while others who have awakened attain enlightenment?
The Master said: "It is not surprising that all people fail to realize it."
The verse says: The celestial wheel shines with perpetual light throughout day and night; that we do not see it is entirely because our eyes are clouded.
There is yet another extraordinary thing: those whose six sense organs are incomplete nevertheless possess the faculty of knowing.
Question: An ancient said, "Do nothing at all; even a Buddha does not act. I do not yet understand what one should do in such a case.
The Master said: "Tsk! Listen—who is it that speaks like this? For now, go and become a Buddha!"
The verse says: Beyond the Name of Awesome Sound lies this single heaven and earth; a single person dwells in a single village.
With unsurpassed nirvana as his companion, he need not divide the household affairs of his simple life.
Question: "In the trichiliocosm, there is no land where his body does not appear. Why then does the Universal Eye seek Samantabhadra and yet fail to see him?
The Master said: "Tsk! It is strange that the Universal Eye seeks Samantabhadra and does not see him; it is even stranger that he does not see himself."
