Born from the womb of Māyā, dying in the city of Kuśinagara; to this day, the hot water remains devoid of emotion, yet it leaves a scar upon the head year after year.
*Bǎnghè* (The Staff and the Shout).
A thousand shouts and ten thousand shouts; striking to the left and striking to the right—these are not for any other extraordinary purpose, but simply to achieve liberation and ease.

Having read the *Recorded Sayings* of Mazu, it is said that "the colt has trampled all under heaven," yet fortunately one remains on Mount Emei. For this reason, I do not begrudge these two stalks [of incense].
Eyebrows: He has turned them over from root to tip and explained it all.
Sweeping away the master’s stupa in a flash—thirty years have passed. One forgets the path by which one came; the green grass is as fresh as ever. The vermilion color has already grown old.

The principle of the fundamental nature remains constant through antiquity and the present; the affairs of formation and destruction are difficult to preserve. Return and depart with no other concern than to sweep the Master’s stupa.
Setting out for my labors, I braved the rain and wind; returning under the stars and amidst the moon, I was unaware of physical suffering, mindful only that my practice might falter.

Wandering the mountains, I briefly departed from the meditation gate to roam the summit. Ten thousand peaks gather emerald hues, opening wide my two eyes. Turning suddenly, I ask those who came with me:
who recognizes the old bhikṣu in the mountains?
I ask: where has the white cloud gone? It follows the wind and accompanies the moon as they enter the hall together.
When asked what words it spoke, each disperses slowly toward the eight directions.
The arrival of the Head Seat (Shouzuo) coincides with the same year and month. From the Sea East and Mountain East to the River North and River North, heaven and earth are in communication;

the life-vein of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is entirely gathered therein. It is essential that the wise guide the ignorant masses: when raising [the Dharma], do not involve yourself; when employing it, do not strike against the edge.

Manifesting as ordinary beings yet responding to the sages, you are wondrously in accord with the profound mystery. Abiding nowhere, you do not encounter anything anywhere. Such is that which transcends the conventional;
it is entrusted to your very person.
The Abbot, whose original name was Benran, composed this verse for him:
"Benran is pure and clear, vast and as it is; He has realized his affinity through many lifetimes. All that meets the eye is harmoniously fused in ultimate subtlety;
Every movement of his entire being is entirely void and mysterious. The ultimate principles of the five schools are simultaneously penetrated; The subtle and profound truths of the Three Baskets—"
Together they are perfected; they do not obstruct the affairs of the ancient and modern, the mundane and the sagely.
The Tathāgata-dhyāna merges with the Patriarchal-dhyāna.

As for the minor Minister Jiu and the three valleys, their shadows vanish because their forms are exhausted. Is it that when the mind is empty, conditions are thereby empty? This has nothing to do with not following the Muni.
The essential point: for the most part, when the mind arises, one cannot avoid error.

Only when heaven and earth are ground to powder is it truly marvelous. If even a wildcat refuses to submit, then even if you were to transcend past, present, and future, you would still not have exhausted even a fraction of your doubt.
Together with the licentiate Yuan Xitai, we have made every place a field of Prajñā.
Every mountain naturally harbors its own white clouds. Each man knows how to turn his body around;
who would be willing to endure carrying a stinking sack?
Together with Imperial Protector Fu Zhen-nan of Jianyang, we do not follow the various sages;
how could we seek [the truth] elsewhere than within our own minds? The hundred flowers bloom and then fall, yet none can distinguish spring from autumn.
With Director of Works Deng Liu’ang:
"In summer and autumn it is often hot; in spring and winter there is much snow and rain. When cold and heat attack one another, even the wise find it difficult to distinguish between them."
In the midst of heat there is cold; in the midst of cold there is heat. Since the Master dwells within both cold and heat, why need one fuss so much?

[The Master] answered Imperial Historian Wang (the Master had lived in the mountains during his youth; the Historian urged him to travel to visit various teachers, whereupon the Master replied with this verse):
"Since my youth, I have found the gruel in the forest sweet; When have I ever intended to emulate the Golden Immortal? The vast, azure sky does not obscure its emptiness."
Truly, one who wishes to fully encompass the most excellent field must discuss the Great Vehicle with Master Deng:

the mountains and rivers of the great earth are entirely without leakage; casting one's body across the universe, all is but empty form. This does not rely on anything beyond the extraordinary to penetrate the profound mystery.
The Essential Meaning: Once joyful, once sorrowful.
Before the withered tree at the crag, divergent paths abound; what then within the sandalwood grove?
Even if one were to mount the back of the golden-haired lion, one must still understand the "Li-lo" chant of the Zen forest.

I send this monk on his travels to inform you that your Zen practice must be genuine. Do not let yourself become like a cloth bag carrying burdens at both ends. Be free and independent, going as the moment dictates;
what matters it whether it is the "three before" or the "three after"?

The *tánhuā* (dharma-flower) blooms profusely for Magistrate Chongzhu, flying everywhere across the heavens; yet it does not enter the single bamboo door of my humble home. I already possess my own set of implements;
why need I further receive the alms-bowl or don the monastic robes?
Having purchased gold, one sells it to others; in the end, all this is but a waste of effort.
One must surely overturn empty space and smash it to pieces before one will no longer have one's eyes changed by others.
Describing his awakening, he sought to enter the path of unsurpassed Bodhi; he hurriedly cleared away the great and fine mountain. Only upon knowing the Way did he realize the mountain was not good;
turning his body around, he passed straight through the Patriarch’s Barrier.
Thoroughly penetrating the universe, one passes the upward barrier; the eyebrows do not intersect with the eyes.
Casting aside both sagehood and ordinariness, life and death alike—one need concern oneself with nothing more than the "three before" and the "three after."

When the ground is suddenly severed, liberation is attained; the obstruction in the breast disperses, and one emerges from the tangle of entanglements. With "zhi-hu-ye-ra," one transcends past and present;
manifesting heaven and earth, this is a realm distinct from the ordinary.
The wild lion does not eat the food of men; on the twelve peaks of Mount Wu, he attains freedom.
Having cultivated the power of unimpeded mastery in all directions, he turns Mount Kunlun upside down to become the Isle of Yingzhou.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* investigates the mind and discriminates vision;

its wondrous purport is entirely and solely the Perfect [Teaching]. The "Investigation of the Mind in Seven Places" serves to eliminate partiality, while the "Discrimination of Vision in Eight Ways" returns one to the True Vision.
Yet, this True Vision has never uttered a single word.
A lion roaming in the mountains has no retinue; this old monk has always cherished solitude. He plants millet in the mountains to sustain his remaining years;
once he has entered the Gate of the School, he shall not enter the secular world again.
A three-bay cottage within the shadows of Ten-Thousand-Pine; a single person before a cliff of withered wood.
For twenty or thirty years one passes like this—would one be willing to trade such profound interest for empty fame?

I describe myself as one whose entire life is lived by the single standard of the staff. Its transformations are boundless, for I must simply follow its lead. Neither Buddhas, patriarchs, nor sages can surpass it;
it is because this eye is upright that dragons and snakes are discerned.
Mountains layer upon layer, and waters flow on and on. What water or mountain could not contain them? Who would not cherish this wondrous, profound realm of awakening?
Yet this old monk regards it as nothing more than a tattered sail.
The Way permeates body and mind, transcending the mundane world; it shatters iron walls and silver mountains.
Casting aside all that the sages and worthies employ, one may freely stride across the barriers of the Buddhas and patriarchs.
The white tuft between his brows constantly emits light; he fears not the thorny stumps of a thousand mountains.
Having clearly distinguished the black from the white, what worry need there be that his conduct does not accord with the Way?
With not a single thing remaining, one wanders in ease; the myriad demons of land and water cannot capture them. Manifesting or concealing according to the mind, they forget grasping and rejecting;
for those who possess wealth, there is ultimately no true elegance.
The Yangtze River in the eighth month has no wind or waves; the great ocean at the three times is devoid of tides.
Meeting such a state as this, even where there is no leisure, one finds leisure.
A Verse on Returning to Master Huibianrong:
Within this, there is neither awakening nor delusion; Illusory manifestations come, and again they return. Coming, it stands upright—who is "I"? Departing, in the end, who am "I"?
It would be better to have no coming and no going; How can one compare this to the arising of conceptual understanding?
Tragic death! Only today do I realize there is neither self nor non-self. Ridden sideways upon the Iron-Faced One, not returning but having returned.
Answering Master Jianfeng:
"Vainly you carry your staff and wooden block to mingle with the mundane dust; how many people are there who truly understand this? To stir up chaos in heaven and earth is no good."
The hand: traversing the universe, its true essence is fundamentally real. Shattering the void, the clay ox bellows; overturning the great ocean, the wooden horse is startled.
The abbot knows nothing of this poor monk’s affairs: he plants his feet beneath the southern mountain and travels across the northern peak.
With Lord Wu Zhan-nan, the Great Way is luminously clear within the mind and eyes.

There is no need for deliberation or to fix the mind upon grasping; contemplating emptiness to enter meditative absorption only leads further away, and chasing after phrases and seeking words makes it increasingly difficult to perceive.
Understanding the meaning and penetrating the profound still leaves one entangled in the net; following the flow to attain the wondrous—[is this not yet sufficient?]
Passing through the barrier: wishing to peer into the profound principle from this point, one must simply let the body and mind die once.
The Verse of Great Penetration says:
"Great Penetration is immediately free from all subtlety; the standards of past and present are entirely untainted; it is simply that which is originally possessed."
Sufficient! It is because within this very place there arises entanglement. To meet on another peak is still not wondrous; to strike the vital point across the shore—how could that be profound?
Even if there were matters concerning the single transmission, one would surely feel aversion toward them.
Four Poems on Dwelling in the Mountains Not dwelling in the realm of sages nor in the cage of the common folk, my natural way of life is unlike that of others.

Though there are no waters of the Three Gorges upon my tongue, within my heart there is a separate wind for a single sail. Elsewhere in all quarters, cremations leave behind traces; here, however, one is buried alive.
A few traces remain. I venture to ask you, traveler from beyond the world: how does this old monk compare to a wood-seller?
When the sentiments of sage and ordinary man are exhausted, the breast is filled with emptiness; with both legs stretched long, let the Master take his ease.

This is neither a deluded traveler lost on the road, nor an old man lying drunk in the street. Merged in suchness, there is no dharma to be conceived; suddenly and brilliantly clear, it is forever beyond [conceptualization].
From beginning to end, waking and sleeping, life and death, are all of one essence.

Nan Neng does not understand the Chan school; he topples empty space to use as a pillow for sleep. Thus, the mountains and waters flow on of their own accord. Although he dwells in the world, how could he ever be of the world?

He takes no pleasure in being born in heaven, yet how could he be apart from heaven? In a single thought, all is suddenly empty—who would discuss the Way? Without a mind, there is silent resonance; who is there to [perceive it]?
Studying Zen: To penetrate heaven and reach the earth is nothing other than this; what need is there to point to the flower to transmit it separately?
On the single path to the profound mystery, few people travel; only those of the highest caliber know its pure flavor.

One does not dwell within the house of the void-natured, nor is one born from among the ranks of the heterodox. This has nothing to do with forced stubbornness or forgetting self and others; it is simply because one distinguishes clearly.
Within the realms of favorable and adverse conditions, firmly grasp the essence of consciousness; naturally, there shall be a distinct "star of the scale" [the true center].

Chanting, one sees that wind and space come and go without anything existing therein; the overturning and formation of worlds occur in a single kṣaṇa. To turn the earth and revolve the heavens requires no effort.

Small indeed; yet the power to overturn rivers and stir the seas remains great. Having passed through the tiger’s den, one hears its deep roar; resting upon the whale-river, one awaits the falling tide.
For those who would return by the supreme *pratyutpanna* samādhi, there is no need to snap the fingers—the single sail will pass.
In verse on the moon:
As clouds disperse across the vast sky, the hare-marked orb hangs suspended. Its light swallows the myriad phenomena; how serene its arising!

It blends seamlessly with the world’s refined and coarse forms, reflecting through rivers and lakes the heavens above and below. Without relying on the lamp of Chan to wander the garden of Dharma, it shines forth like the Buddha-fire.
Golden Lotus. Master Ma once boasted among the multitude beyond the mundane world; Old Wang was able to transcend the ocean of the *Tripiṭaka*.

Dwelling in the mountains, living in poverty, the wilds were devoid of surplus grain. Only the bright moon and clear wind accompanied his grass mat. A single brazier of firewood and a bowl full of radish soup.
The alms bowl; dwelling in tranquility, one does not contend with the world’s fluctuations of heat and cold.
With a tattered robe, wind and snow pierce through to chill the skin; hands folded, one sits by the hearth facing the dead embers. Is it that Heaven is partial and afflicts me alone?
No—the Dharma-body is frozen, yet it cannot kill the Tathāgata.
When traveling the mountains to study the Way, do not distinguish between kin and stranger. He is now me, and I am not he. There is a distinct flavor to traveling the mountains;
when the karmic consciousness drags one along, one must become a donkey.

I admonish those who indulge in worldly pleasures: let the practitioner of the Way forget such indulgence. Be simple and follow conditions as they arise; the wise and accomplished can rest content with their lot, while the ignorant and deluded do nothing but resent Heaven.

Lying on firewood and tasting gall to discipline oneself, one finds even drinking water sweet. If one truly acts for the sake of birth and death, one will wear a robe of lotus fibers, mending it until it is threadbare.
Baofang exhorts the assembly:
"The path before one’s door is not the wondrous way; seeing with eyes that lack pupils is even clearer.
If you study the Way but cannot transcend the stage of learning, your iron shoes will wear through in vain, to no avail."
To show the Chan practitioner:
"Pressing emptiness against emptiness—its merit is great; having a pursuit and having an attainment—its virtue remains slight.
To slander Kāśyapa’s state of natural ease is to lose what was gained at the very moment one found advantage. (When Boshan first entered the room, the Master showed him this verse.)
Reluctant to indulge the mind in seeking out external paths, for it is because the Great Function possesses its own livelihood.
This present matter of refined elegance can be understood only by the veteran masters of the Zen groves.

If you wish to attain a state where the entire body is entirely mouth, it is most fitting to pierce through everything at once beneath the Patriarchal School. Unless the Zen barrier is shattered, how can there be peace?
Turn it over directly, and the waves will strike the heavens.
On the path of awakening, who does not traverse it? Yet one must take each step with fresh spontaneity. Throughout the ten directions and the three realms, there is no barrier of dust;
the great earth, mountains, and rivers have no boundaries.
Picking up Mount Sumeru to question the azure sky—how could one know that Śūnyatā would discern the wind? Having turned his body, he has already entered the vast ocean;
yet how can he avoid his eyebrows weighing down his two pupils?
The Dharma-gates are wide open everywhere; yet though they accord with principle and meet the capacity, one cannot enter. Do not believe me?
Just look at the three ancient Buddhas, who were forced to turn back only after being struck by a great illness.
Having purchased gold, he sells it to others; he breaks open the void and hands it to one who knows its sound. The pure breeze does not permit passage through the gate;
why need the stone maiden inquire whether things are old or new?
Yunmen spoke of a "Mount Sumeru" to the two lay practitioners of Fuzhou; those who travel the direct path instead take a detour.
Only Liaoyuan has traveled the straight way, yet he did not ascend the barrier of the ancestral masters of old.
Fayan traveled in various quarters and his insights were many; yet they could not compare to the finger-tip of Dizang. One must press through until the very bones of empty space are shattered;
only then does one understand that all things are already fully manifest, and only then can one truly defecate.

Manifesting the natural radiance of the original ground, the Chan practitioner’s stillness pervades the Dharma-realm; throughout the ten directions, all is pure and free from even a speck of dust. Encompassing heaven and wrapping around earth, there is not a single thing;
the traditions of Śākya, Daoism, and Confucianism are but empty names.

Showing that Yuanzhu, the Master of the Pass, attained realization through having its causes and conditions, and that awakening occurs at the proper time: "The green mountains bloom in fragrance once every year;
if one can simply not be driven by the passage of time, one will naturally accord with the mechanism of transformation."
The myriad dharmas are gathered back into the one dharma; meeting people and meeting things, there is only this single stroke. He goes the eastern road while I go the western;
straightening and opening up their intersection, it is beyond appraisal.
This matter has never been permitted from the outset. Indeed, it is difficult to find even ten people who succeed. One must cause branches to grow upon branches;
only then can one understand walking with hands cast off over a precipice.
Showing the state of the ancestral Way among the Chan practitioners of Shaoshi:
how has it declined? Because they do not accord with the truth, they mock the dhūtas. On the peaks of solitary crags, those who give rise to true vitality are few;

within the tides of the great ocean, those who die are many. How many can truly grasp the surging waves and seize the clouds? To overturn heaven and strip the earth—[who can do this? *Note: The final phrase "莫" (mò) is left as a fragmentary ending, suggesting the text may be incomplete or intentionally elliptical.*
Seeking others, one must know the affairs before Mount Shaoshi. By following faith and the divine light, one reaches Bodhidharma.
He showed that the fundamental nature of dhyāna practitioners is the original suchness;
phenomena arise according to conditions following delusion, but by knowing delusion, one returns to the truth. Investigating this truth, there is neither beginning nor end.

Having reached this source of truth and delusion, encompassing heaven and enveloping earth, one clearly understands the traces of causes and conditions to be like the beginning and end of dreams and illusions.
Birth and death are likewise thus; what is there to discard and what is there to grasp? Embarking upon the boat of Prajñā, one simultaneously benefits and delivers both self and others.
The Way shown is as it was from the beginning;

a man of filial integrity and virtue may truly trust in this. One must see through all phenomena. Standing with one’s head to the heavens and feet on the earth, there is a single perfect luminosity—ultimately neither person nor self.
What crime or what merit? Who is good and who is evil? Responding to conditions and engaging with beings is fundamentally thus, pervading everywhere.
The realm pervades all directions as a single entity;

this shows that for the Chan practitioner Yuanying, learning the Way is easy, while governing the mind is difficult. If the mind is governed, why worry that the Way will not transform? The wise investigate the mind, not their learning.

Cutting off study, the empty mind penetrates the Patriarchs’ barrier. Having attained the essential meaning, the Dharma-realm is vast; all worldly contrivances are entirely irrelevant. Not a single dharma is retained, so there is no entanglement;
one transcends and passes through the mountains of self and others. When one dharma is realized, all dharmas are empty.
Suddenly forgetting the five schools and three sects, there is revealed alone the perfectly round light, shining and blazing. Let it be as it is, whether true or false, different or the same—
thus I show it to you, Chan practitioner Ziming.
Worthy of release, not fit for gathering; clearly knowing the end of the dark path. Refusing to traverse the bright road, how could one allow wandering in the shadows?

Knowing the traces of bubbles by playing in the water, reaching the seclusion of the realm by climbing the mountain. Like drifting clouds upon surging waves, one attains spontaneous leisure in emptiness.
The Heart-Moon of Master Yinjiang reflects the clarity of the river above and below; penetrating heaven and piercing earth, it is ultimately difficult to fathom.

Lofty yet remaining in the depths, it is as tranquil as it is within active function. Birth and extinction do not interfere with its traceless, empty response; coming and going do not involve any duality.
The traces of these names have been clarified; reaching this point is truly sublime. In every object, as it meets the opportune moment, all places are the same.
To instruct the Chan practitioner Wukong: one must awaken to original emptiness.
Do not allow yourself to be ensnared by the "emptiness" of so-called "true emptiness" or by form and color. Once awakened, there is no birth, for birth and death have ceased.

Quiescence. Penetrating through to the fundamental nature, form and emptiness are fused; from emptiness arises great awakening like a bubble surfacing. From awakening emerges void clarity like the crimson sun.
Yet there is another transmitted essence of the school’s intent: walking south while facing north, one calls out to the mountain elder.
To Layman Fu of Jianyang I show:
a pure, clear, and pristine single spiritual light. In every land and every atom, nothing is concealed. Myriad upon myriad, all have lost their awareness;
much and little alike, they do not reflect. Bright and clear, there is no birth or death; going and coming, it does not...
Severing both permanence and annihilation, and treating right and wrong as if they were a dream, one truly and authentically takes up the burden with joy.
To the assembly of Chan practitioners in the hall, he showed that the Great Way is ineffable;
yet the Way is not revealed by silence. When the Master encountered Danxia, a single push turned him completely around.
The Great Way cannot be scrutinized; if one does not scrutinize it, the Way will not be attained. Miaoxi’s cage was shattered by Shao, who thereby came to know the nature of things.
The Great Way cannot be debated; if one does not debate it, the Way will not be clarified. Luopu met Jia Shan, and only after being struck did he finally submit to his teachings.
The Great Way cannot be looked back upon; if one does not look back, one does not awaken. The Hermitage Master turned away from Yunju, thus missing his mother’s birth-clothes.
To the Xitang Zen practitioner who has finished his inquiry:
"What is the matter within? Where there is no wind or water, waves are produced. Turning back the chaos of heaven and earth to repay the ancestors.

Virtue! To lift up "Namo Sittadha" and show the Chan practitioner Lingran that he wishes to walk hand-in-hand with the former patriarchs, one must first turn one's body within the thorny brambles; furthermore, one must be able to stride upon the golden-haired lion.
Turning his back, he began to believe that his full majesty neither diminished nor increased.

To the scholar Huang Yuangong, he showed that the spirit and bearing of a true man is like that of a king. Grasping at empty space, he performed a scene; in an instant, the karmic conditions of heaven were suddenly activated.
It arises. The great function of the entire body is spontaneously assumed.
To show Yuanxian:

each time one penetrates through, it becomes deeper and deeper. From of old, Buddhas and Patriarchs have not permitted anyone; even if you were to mount the golden-maned lion, [you would still not be allowed].
Turn your back! I also teach that one must turn oneself over beneath the staff.

To the Zen practitioner who seeks to clarify the mind, I show that clarifying the mind is easy, but deadening the mind is difficult. When the mind is deadened, the environment becomes naturally tranquil. Cut down the vermilion cassia tree in the moon.
The Shadow: Transversely crossing, he knocks down the patriarchal barrier.

For the practitioner Tianran, the golden furnace reveals the true and the false; having undergone many blows from the tongs and hammer, the more so does his newness appear. With transformations without fixed direction, he becomes a vessel.
Usage: To casually bring it forth and startle the multitude of heroes.
Showing the monks at night retreat:
they don their robes and sit in meditation upon the couch throughout the night, silently listening as the bitter frost falls from the void. The north wind through the crack of the door is truly like—
The arrow. How many people reaching this point are willing to take it up?
Dong Yan urges the assembly to practice with genuine effort.
When the sentiments of sagehood and ordinariness are exhausted, there is nothing. One must die within the living; after death, one awaits the revival.
It is much like drifting clouds dispersing; it is just like the solitary bright moon. Its radiance pervades the entire Dharma-realm, sitting firmly as the ancient Vairocana.
Exhorting Chan Master Tan:

"With sincerity held fast for ten thousand miles, it is a single piece of iron—no matter how clever one may be, it cannot accommodate its two ends. Even if the Mara-king Devadatta were to exert all his power,"
Set it aside. You need only cast it into the furnace like snow.
Exhort Yuan Taixue:
A true man of great character must see through this. Human life is like a temporary lodging; one merely borrows it for a single night. When dawn breaks, one must depart.
It may be so; yet ultimately, one moves ever forward. Cause and effect cannot avoid falling away. Having long abandoned one’s ancestral home, one knows not how to return;
wandering aimlessly along the roads, all is error.

Great man, you should understand for yourself: as long as one has a body, one will never reach full understanding. Though one may exhaustively read the books of a hundred kings, one cannot avoid being subjected to flogging and torture.
Yet, with a single invocation of "Namo Buddha," all have already attained the Way of the Buddhas. Heaven and hell do not interfere with one another;
since there is fundamentally no self, one must strive for liberation while still young.
Addressing the Assembly on New Year’s Eve:
The kalpas have already met with years of famine; On this New Year’s day, do not begrudge the thinness of the gruel.
A man of iron liver and stone bones, devoid of sentiment— Once sated, he sits upright and forgets a hundred hungers.

The Zen practitioner Chezong requested instruction on the "Single-Framework Meditation" practiced day and night: "Body and mind are entirely tranquil; there is only a luminous clarity that universally manifests throughout the ten directions."
I have not yet seen the Buddhas or Patriarchs; what need is there to speak of sages or immortals? What dharma or Way could I possibly discuss?

I have investigated their mysteries and Zen, but find only the Empty Old Master who shares a great affinity with me. He accompanies me in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down; he stays with me as we sleep together.
I know his coming and going; he recognizes my original source. At times he provokes and vexes me, seizing a single vajra-ring.

This is not the "holding up of a flower" demonstration; how could one know there was a separate transmission? Once one awakens to its essential principle, one suddenly emerges from the shroud of delusion.
Transcending far beyond the bounds of past and present, where could he not find peace?
Residing on a towering peak amidst yellow pines, Layman Xixi requested instruction from the Master.

Dwelling in this world, he was not of this world; his conduct and reclusion were utterly distinct from the common way. He bid farewell to his kin, severed his attachments, and withdrew into the wilderness.
I plow with knives and sow by fire for my livelihood; I have had little instruction from teachers in studying Chan and the Way.
When I bow to the Buddha or meet others, I offer one extra prostration. I do not attend vegetarian feasts nor solicit alms; I do not associate with the wealthy nor draw near to the noble.
All day long I am busy—how could I fall into idleness? Day and night I remain alert—how could I sleep? Constantly pressing together this single sphere, I block off the dust of the senses.
The paths of the emotional, the monastic, and the secular are not based on the Buddha or the sages, nor are they based on oneself; they do not rely on new rules, nor do they rely on old ones.
On the first three and the eleventh, all conceptual deliberation ceases; in the middle nine and the lower seven, there is no mutual exchange.

Others find joy in the state of non-action, yet I still give rise to fear in this state of non-action. This profound pit at the bottom of serene liberation—this is precisely where one must awaken through practice.
Shift the pivot and look upward; take another step from the top of the hundred-foot pole. Treading upon the head of a dead cat, all that was previously possessed is now entrusted.
It is not merely a matter of acting recklessly or in vain; for the most part, it is because one has understood how to look after [the Way] in past lives.
The Buddhas and Patriarchs are like withered stumps; the Dharma-way and the vehicle of the lineage have become a mere public proclamation. These are but idle words and leftover talk.

Descending into the human realm, there is no need to seek any further "profound depths. Now that the weather is cold, I ask for instruction and express my innermost feelings; I do not dare indulge in idle chatter to provoke the displeasure of others.
May this serve as a warning against dullness and torpor.
Throughout the births and deaths of the three realms, the five desires share a single course; yet among all things of desire, there is one that stands supreme: the Demon King of Sleep.
His supernatural powers are nearly equal to those of the Buddha, and his influence pervades the world without concealment. Yet he does not dwell upon the earth, nor does he reside in the heavens.
Coming like wind driving mist, departing like lightning flashing light; once it has entered a human body, one leans against the wall and collapses onto the bed.
Disregarding both body and life, one cares not for father or mother; rejecting all wealth and treasures, one cares not for fields or manors.
The karmic deeds of this world have already passed away, yet within dreams one creates new calamities. Following the conditions of good or evil, there may be what is wholesome or unwholesome;

one indulges in killing, stealing, lust, and falsehood, throwing into chaos the laws, regulations, and eternal constants. The benefits and harms are beyond words, all arising from the loss of self-mastery.
A man of character should awaken early and seek a place of peace and joy. Investigating until reaching the ultimate limit, all is termed the Constant Light of Tranquility (*sada-prabhāsvara*).
Since neither sage nor ordinary being fundamentally exists, who can truly uphold names and forms? The three realms are but a single dream; let the wise be diligent in their precautions.

Originally there is nothing at all; it simply requires understanding through investigation and deliberation. A flash of insight must still be exerted with effort; once awakened, cease all discursive thought.
Among those who have been lucid throughout past and present, none can compare to the Great Awakened King. You practitioners of the Buddha-way and guests who study Zen: do not let this time slip away.
For nine years he sat facing the wall; for six years he dwelt in the Snowy Mountains. White mold grew upon his lips, yet his mind remained as adamantine as diamond.

All this was solely for the sake of this one matter, so that his name might be celebrated through the ages. He broke down the fortress of the Demon King; in capturing a thief, one must recover the stolen goods.
The Buddha is a dried dung-heap; the Sangha is an old withered stump; the Dharma is paper for sores; Zen is Old Man Meng.
When one travels through the various quarters and arrives here, only then has one reached home. Yet one must further know there is the "phrase after the last":
look closely at the willow catkins chasing the setting sun.
The Master sat in meditation atop Mount E’feng and was moved by this realization:
Amidst the vast and boundless four seas, who possesses a heart as firm as iron? Were it not for an iron-hearted resolve, how could the wild mind ever be stilled?
When Yaoshan saw Shitou, the head of the matter was split into two pieces; had he not met Mazu Daoshi, the spine of the iron ox would have been severed.
To realize this field of rest, the paths of the patriarchs and Buddhas diverge; dwelling in mountain forests wherever one may be, one must still employ the three strips of bamboo.
Majestic is the great man; each has their own place of origin. A thousand sages have not transmitted it, yet how could ten thousand dharmas ever cease?
Seeking from antiquity to the present, none can compare to the wisdom of this *dhūta*. With a single laugh, the ocean of Buddhas dries up—yet even to this day, it remains unfathomably deep.
If one wishes to cause the ocean to dry up, one must simply make the mind like iron.

Entrusting this to Boshan, who lazily straddles the horn of the blue dragon—what need is there to hope for the moon-jewel? This is not because the matter cannot be resolved; it is only for fear of wasting effort.
He said to the scholar Huang Zian:

"A man of great character will by no means remain muddled. When the light returns and shines back, it pierces through [delusion]; originally there are not two. This is the sudden faculty of superior wisdom."
It is utterly beyond thought. It shatters the vajra-ring; it is like encountering a born enemy. Only when one has grasped the very core can it be called a true arrival.
I do not dare to indulge in flowery speech, for this is direct and straightforward; I entrust it to the gentleman, who should be cautious regarding this.
Spontaneously Composed While Sitting at Night in Dongyan:
Tonight I have entered the *nāga*-samādhi; The entire dharma-realm is purely and utterly clear. All Buddhas of the ten directions are likewise so;
Monks throughout the world realize this together. It is not on earth, nor does it dwell in heaven; It abides neither in empty space nor in the profound beyond.
Mysterious! For immeasurable kalpas it has been exactly thus; neither hastened nor delayed. This samādhi is fundamentally without entering or exiting.
Realizing the practice of the Prajñāpāramitā, the ocean of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Great Vaipulya Buddha emerges from this.
The profound discourse of the Tripiṭaka is originally non-dual; how could the hundred schools and various masters not be one? It is simply because of...
A single thought of a person differs; a thousand transformations and ten thousand changes follow divergent paths. To penetrate into this school is called the most supreme;
herein it is termed "applying effort. This is shown to the practitioners of Zen.

The wandering of the patch-robed monks is utterly distinct from that of other students; they take wondrous awakening as their goal. They shatter the barriers of the patriarchs and tread upon the pavilion of Vairocana.
They swallow the thorny *karkaṭaka* fruit and don the tattered rags of a hundred fragments. They travel where there is no path and pass through the brambles.

Speech is not talking; silence is not sitting. In phenomena there is no discrimination; in principle there is no deliberation. Penetrating the sea and piercing the clouds, not a single drop can adhere.
When mountains and peaks come all at once, there is nothing with which to settle. One does not see the wrongness of the ordinary; one simply verifies the transcendence of the sage.
Requiting virtue and protecting life, one is not constrained by good or evil; pervading the entire Dharma-realm, it is difficult to describe or fathom.

Even the Buddha has no recourse but to speak extensively of cause and effect, yet for such a person, hell and heaven do not even exist in their dreams. Whether shouting or rebuking, they move with total freedom and expansive openness.
It does not flow constantly; who can grasp it? When the waves of consciousness stirred by the hidden wind return to stillness, above and below merge entirely into Great Perfect Enlightenment.
Thus he instructs the practitioners of Chan.

The single path of the Chan school must be personally realized. Once realization has come, one walks alone in the vast expanse. Words do not touch upon thought; the essential meaning does not involve commentary.
When Buddhas and demons appear before you, how can there be room for dispute? It is like wielding the Ganjiang sword: whoever encounters it dies instantly.
It is like a great mass of fire; those who approach it find it difficult to guard against. To receive this before the pivot of the teaching is not the mark of a clever disciple.

Only when it is revealed after the words can one truly be counted among them. Knowing there is that which transcends the upward path, and believing in this reality, one does not involve oneself in verbal explanations, but is directly and utterly revealed.

To speak without skillful means is to fall away from the path of meaning. To realize that this is not profound is likewise to have no place of realization. Sweeping away all traces and cutting off all footprints requires the Master of Masters.
Miscellaneous Writings:
A Dharma Talk Requested by Zen Practitioners.
Generally speaking, this Way prizes genuine practice. When truth is engraved upon the mind, the Way will manifest of itself. Even if...

Their minds are insincere. Though they may ascend to the hall once a day and discourse on the Way without ceasing for a moment, this serves merely as a pretext for conversation and ultimately provides no benefit to the Way. What, then, is meant by "reality"?

It lies in reflecting inwardly during daily activities so that one's own mind remains pure and untainted by any form of improper corruption. For the mind is like a monkey, and the intellect is likewise...
The horse is not bound by the tethers and reins of great awakening and illumination; it is truly difficult to subdue through its divine mechanisms alone.

Only when subjected to a thousand lashes and ten thousand interrogations does it submit and descend, melting back into the single mark where the traces of arising and ceasing are severed. Thereupon, one naturally awakens to the fundamental wondrous luminosity.

Vastly penetrating and spiritually unimpeded, phenomena and mind are one and the same, with no superfluous dharma remaining. When speech and action both accord with ultimate impartiality, only then can one be said to have a heart that does not deceive.
At the moment when the heart does not deceive, all worldly and world-transcending dharmas are the Buddha-dharma;
whether the mind arises or does not arise, it is always the Buddha-mind. Thus it is said: "In the ground of ultimate reality, not even a single speck of dust is received," and yet...

The Samādhi of Dust upon Dust: within the gateway of the myriad practices, not a single dharma is abandoned, yet every dharma is entirely true. Formerly, the World-Honored One closed his chamber in Magadha;
Vimalakīrti displayed silence in Vaiśālī. This was a complete and total presentation of the pure and singular truth, leaving even the sages and worthies at a loss for words.
When Shancai gathered common weeds to make medicine, they could both kill and bring people to life;
when Niaoke blew on a tuft of cloth to instruct others, it led them to ultimate penetration and realization. When Nanyue ground a brick to make a mirror, he resolved Mazu’s thirty-year Zen impasse.
The Fourth Patriarch wrote to the Buddha to provide him with fullness; Huineng and Daorong exhausted their lifelong skills.
Baizhang received a single shout, which left his ears deaf for three days; Huangbo employed three blows of the staff, which caused a thousand mechanisms to thunder forth.
Under a single word, one casts off the binding vines of ten thousand kalpas; within silence, one breaks free from the karmic net of a thousand lifetimes. Words and language—
It is flavorless, like a soup made from boiled wood chips; it would require a divine power to consume it, resembling rice cooked from iron nails.

Unless one possesses great fundamental wisdom, it is truly difficult to swallow. Although those of the dragon-elephant lineage are difficult to fathom, there are those with the auspicious sprouts of spiritual potential who naturally excel.

Without being constrained by formal rules, yet upholding the Dharma during the final age, one thoroughly investigates its source; all of this arises from within a single, true, and wondrous realization.
Zen practitioner, request a discourse on the Dharma.
Originally, those who truly investigate and authentically awaken must first strike at their own selves, causing the innate, luminous clarity to shine forth.

Subsequently, they must encounter a person to thoroughly penetrate the "bar-nose" (the essential pivot) of the Ultimate; they must master the subtle essentials of existence and non-existence, wherein both grasping and rejecting are empty.

They must transcend the mysterious mechanism of gain and loss, making honor and disgrace one and the same. Where there is no place for exertion, they resolve birth and death and proceed with spontaneous freedom.
Come! To be free from mental effort is to penetrate the truth of both the mundane and the sacred; there is no obstruction regarding superiority or inferiority.
Even if Deshan’s blows fall like raindrops, they do not touch the shadow of one's spine; even if Linji’s shouts roar like thunder, they do not reach the strings of one's ears.

This is not out of arrogance, but is the natural style of our own house. To the millions of humans and devas, he displayed the *tāṇḍava* flower; with a single transmission and a single laugh, he [manifested] the dragon and the elephant.
Thousands upon thousands have exhausted themselves in the non-dual, yet only this one was granted the permission of wordlessness. Transmitting mind-to-mind, it is like a mirror meeting a mirror.
It reveals a direct and unerring course, free from any subtle contrivance. Riding upon compassionate vows, he steers the vessel across the ocean of Dharma;
relying on his sovereign freedom, he throws open the pivot of the ancestral temple. At such a moment, the tongue is rendered speechless, and names and words are cast aside.
Rest. This may be called true inquiry.

Regarding the essentials of the Buddha-remembrance practice (*buddhānusmṛti*), the one who practices Buddha-remembrance must have a pure mind. With a pure mind, practice Buddha-remembrance; with a pure mind, listen. The mind is the Buddha, and the Buddha is the mind.

Attaining Buddhahood is nothing other than the purity of mind and meditative concentration. Those who practice the mindfulness of the Buddha must be diligent; when pure mindfulness continues without interruption, one attains Buddhahood before others.
The Buddha-body pervades the entire Dharma-realm; this single thought-moment without deviation is the Supreme Vehicle. With the mind mindful of the Buddha, all doubt is severed.

When doubt is completely purified, that is Bodhi. Moment after moment, nothing arises; there is no bondage or entanglement. Throughout the ten directions and the three realms, there is universal radiance.

Mind is Buddha; Buddha is mind. All phenomena return to the one, the living flame. From within the light of this living flame, a unique sprout emerges, naturally not falling into the various expedient means.
The mind that recollects the Buddha is the Pure Land; the pure mind is the locus upon which all Buddhas rely.

Abiding thus, the mind that recollects the Buddha surpasses all myriad conditions; in the empty mind, one swiftly ascends the path of non-arising. One who recollects the Buddha must have a correct mind;
a correct mind is like a crystal mirror, where the ten directions are bright and pure, and nothing can escape it. The myriad phenomena of the universe are the seal upon the ground of the mind.
One who recollects the Buddha must be earnest; with an earnest mind recollecting the Buddha, the wild mind ceases. Once the wild mind has ceased, the Buddha...
Manifest before one’s eyes, its radiance is like the moon in a clear pool; though waves surge and roll, they do not interfere with one another.

The manifestations of sages and ordinary beings are free from birth and death. Contemplate the Buddha-mind and listen for the right moment; when that moment arrives, the mind is naturally joyful, as if caught in a net.
The Great San Pass is broken open like a pearl lost and sought; the Yellow River is taught to run dry. To see such inconceivable benefit is not for the sake of idle chatter, but for you I speak it.
As for the mind of Buddha-remembrance, one must investigate it with fierce intensity. Directly within this remembrance, pursue that which is inherently present.
One does not become a Buddha by means of Buddha-remembrance; the Buddha-nature is pervasive and eternally imperishable. Raising your eyebrows, you must look for yourself.
In a fleeting glance, one sees intimately and forgets former faults. For those who practice the Buddha-remembrance, there is a cause and condition. Faith does not act as a companion to dharmas;

whether meditating on Zen or expounding the teachings, they disregard them entirely. When the mind is clarified through directness, one simply rests. A cow on open ground plows across the great earth;

a net cast across the heavens gathers in the *xiūlóu* (mythical beasts). Capturing them alive and seizing them with vigor, they bring awe to the world—transcending the patriarchs and surpassing the lineage. This is extraordinary.
At the Head of the Road: A Universal Exhortation to Those Who Practice Nianfo and Chan Meditation Do not regard your kinsmen as enemies.
Song of the Stinking Skin Bag (Composed while residing at the Henan Provincial Office) This stinking skin bag will not last long.
In the life of man, do not flaunt your power and strength. Whether one becomes a king, a minister, a commoner, or a soldier— All are but transient roles within this fleeting existence.
Once this dream of impermanence has been fully realized, cease all deliberation. Each follows the workings of destiny as time passes.
Within heaven and earth lies the intent of the Benevolent One (Nenrin), which enables people of this age to escape from suffering and calamity. Now I ask you: what is this intent?
Ultimately, from what source should one take [anything]? The wise person deeply knows this wondrous mind. This spirit is subtle and marvelous, beyond compare.

It does not cover the heavens, nor does it support the earth; what need is there to reckon with the myriad phenomena of the universe? Vast, empty, and profound, it has been so from antiquity until now.
Who would say that birth and death, or coming and going, truly exist? Great Men, you should set your resolve: if you do not awaken to this mind, you will achieve nothing at all.
It is so. To contemplate the cycle of saṃsāra is truly pitiable; one must urgently enter the Way and avoid it. As for this method of avoidance, seek it quickly for yourself.
A single thought of non-arising explains everything; it breaks forth as the true, eternal Great Nirvāṇa. Perfectly luminous, silent, and illuminating, it solidifies heaven and earth.
Although you may see it clearly and distinctly, you must also encounter the "final word" from a person. As for this final word—if...

What is it? When our Buddha held up a flower to show the assembly, the millions of humans and devas were utterly at a loss. Kāśyapa gave a subtle smile to trigger the potential; three thousand and seven hundred cases remain as they were in the past.

All must penetrate the direction and return to the source. Such matters— [Note: The original Chinese text contains a poetic, Zen-style prose. The translation aims to preserve the rhythm and philosophical tone while remaining faithful to the meaning.]

Cutting off language, one reaches home entirely without involving causes and conditions. Śāriputra sat in vain within his cave; Subhūti’s existence was merely for the sake of his hundred daily verses.
It cannot be attained through wisdom or ability; I have never engaged in the profound discourses of the Tripiṭaka.

The unexcelled Way of suchness in a single thought—how could the nine schools or the three teachings ever reach it? To discuss suchness in terms of existence and non-existence, existence is not the myriad things.

All phenomena are like illusions; there is nothing that is not empty, yet there is no nihilistic annihilation. By realizing the skillful means of existence and non-existence, one dwells in eternal companionship with the ancient Vairocana.
Transcending the three realms and leaving the path of delusion, one need not rely on former models.

Understanding how to lead the diverse classes from within their differences, one flows with the current, whether moving with or against it, remaining naturally solitary. As a monk, one is unattached; as a layperson, what need is there for constraint? Throughout all time...

He is able to act where no one else encounters him; standing like a sheer cliff a thousand fathoms high, he is difficult to approach. When they gallop together and offer shouts of praise, what is this? His words have bone; his application is non-action.

Amidst ten thousand distinctions and a thousand differences, he responds spontaneously to the moment. Neither upholding nor violating, he is free from constraints. He slays Buddhas, burns scriptures, and shatters the net of doubt.
Only with such great skillful means does he dare to let loose. This cannot be transmitted otherwise; it is not for those who are not of the Śākya clan. To break [the barriers].
Place the "transmitting lamp" within the sand basin; in the great and wondrous mountains, awaken from the world’s dream.

After awakening, it seems as if one has never been so before—how different this is from ten thousand deaths and a thousand births! It is solely because one does not accord with the principle of non-arising that love and hatred arise life after life.
Love and hate are exhausted; there is only this single spirit. To be thus transparently clear—what person is this? Such ultimate words are difficult to comprehend;
they bring a laugh to Namo Avalokiteśvara.
A Text for Self-Congratulation at Seventy Years of Age.
I reverently reflect that this illusory body, aged and decrepit, has reached the age of seventy. With diligent and earnest effort, I have pursued deep cultivation based on my resolve for learning.
Beholding the profound depth of Prajñā, a resolute mind was suddenly awakened; entering the samādhi of non-abiding, I perceive form as it truly is.
This is emptiness. Surveying the ultimate pinnacle of the *zongcheng* (the core vehicle), he resolved his will to investigate it thoroughly, attaining a subtle and meticulous discernment.

This "non-being" is precisely "being. As the conditions for his awakening were about to ripen, he encountered the vast, primordial, and natural state. Having passed through the great mountain, it was like a spoon opening a lock;
in an instant, he tasted the water of Caodong, which was like cool curd refreshing the heart. Ascending the hall of Linji, he vied for the sweet taste of the staff.
"Ho! Stepping into Yunmen’s chamber, how could one grasp his "Gu-yi"? Entering the hall of Guiyang’s gate, one does not wade into the thousand-fathom well.
Treading upon the quarters of Fayan, there is no interference within the span of two fingers. For nearly thirty years, he secluded himself at Mount E’er and Baofang to cultivate the grain;
for over twenty autumns, he wandered freely with staff in hand across the lakes and seas at Shouchang.

Sitting in the abbot’s quarters while grasping at flowers in the sky brings much reproach to those who follow; ascending the meditation seat while seeking the moon in the water still burdens those who have come before.
As retreats are held in various monasteries, all manner of conditions converge; one’s reputation spreads throughout the various regions like the interlocking teeth of a row of lips.
Suspicions arise from killing through superficiality; one must run the heels across the four seas to investigate gain and loss and examine the ancient wonders of coming and going.

Those who can laugh away their doubts are fellow practitioners; those whose conduct and concealment are extraordinary dwell together only with those who have forgotten words. Throughout the day, they simply wear their robes and eat their meals.

Nakedly pure, one endures hunger; constantly awaiting guests and welcoming visitors. Talkative to the point of forgetting words, one attains such inconceivability that one may simply let the tiger roar and the dragon cry.
All things are accomplished as an inexhaustible treasury of subtlety; one follows freely as the elephant returns and the lion roars.
Thus the life-vein of the Patriarchs flows on, and the nostrils of the sages and worthies are revealed—the esoteric purport of the separate transmission.
It should be at this very moment that the void becomes finite and vast praise falls short;

with utmost sincerity, we look up and pray that the Old Monk may dwell in Amitābha’s Land, universally benefiting humans and devas, and that those who possess the higher mechanism of the Treasury may all, both monastics and laypeople alike, receive his grace.

Epitaph for the Great Master Wuming of Shouchang (with Preface) The Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is like the vast void;
it has been thus from time immemorial and cannot be clarified by the alternation of day and night.
Obscure! Only those who attain it are like those who have obtained a wish-fulfilling jewel; its application is inexhaustible. Its inconceivable power is inherently complete within one's nature;
one receives this clarity within the mind without depending on external things. Among the patriarchs of antiquity, there were none who were not thus. Why is it that in recent times they are so few?
It is not that there is no Chan; it is simply that there are no teachers. Is it truly that there are none? Regarding this, I [have observed] at Shouchang...
The Chan Master has been identified. I have carefully examined the formal report: The Master’s name was Huìjīng; his style name was Wúmíng.

He was the son of the Pèi family of Chóngrén, Fǔzhōu. Initially, there were difficulties during his birth; his grandfather recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, whereupon delivery was achieved.

Consequently, he was named Jīng (Sūtra). From birth, he was exceptionally gifted and unlike others; his appearance was ancient and dignified, like a wild crane soaring through the air. By nature, he was serene and free from worldly attachments.
"Very well. At nine years of age, he entered the local school and immediately asked, "What is this 'vast and unyielding spirit' (*hao-ran zhi qi*)?

The teacher marveled at him. He lived his life as one who seemed indifferent to the affairs of the human world. At seventeen, he abandoned his brush and inkstone, resolutely setting his mind on the Way.
At twenty-one, he happened to enter the residence of a lay practitioner (*jushi*) and saw the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* upon a desk; he read it and—
The volume concludes. Overjoyed, as if having recovered a long-lost object, he immediately spoke of his intention to the scholar. The scholar marveled at this.

From that point on, the Master renounced meat and wine and resolved upon his aspiration for world-transcendence. His parents gave their consent. At that time, Chan Master Zhong Yunkong was preaching the Dharma at Lingshan;
the Master went there to rely upon him. He took the master’s original name, Huijing, and served him for three years. All...
He followed his instructions without opposition, as if he were a simpleton. He had long harbored doubts regarding the four-line verse of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
One day, seeing a verse by Fu Taishi which read: "If one discusses the four-line verse, it should never depart from the body," the Master suddenly felt a sense of liberation.
He then composed a verse containing the line, "Light radiates throughout the entire realm. From this, it is known that his prior cultivation of the *Prajñāpāramitā* had been awakened.

At the age of twenty-four, one day while reading the Tripitaka, he reached the "Chapter on the Eye of the School" (*Zongyan pin*) and only then came to know of the principle of the "special transmission outside the teachings.
Upon reaching the section on the distinctions between the five schools, he harbored secret doubts. He remained in a state of confusion for eight months;

when people thought he was dull-witted because he appeared indifferent to what he heard or saw, after a long time he attained a realization. Thereupon, he developed a fervent resolve to investigate the truth through meditation.

He then took his leave of Lingshan, intending to lead a life of seclusion. He traveled to Mount E’feng and, finding its groves and valleys profound and secluded, he cleared away the brush to establish a dwelling.
He vowed not to reveal the Great Matter until it was resolved, and would never descend from this mountain. After three years had passed, no one knew of his presence there.

While reading the *Transmission of the Lamp*, the Master saw a monk ask Xingshan, "What is the Way? Xingshan replied, "A magnificent mountain. The Master was at a loss, and doubt suddenly arose within him.
Day and night he held this to mind, forgetting even sleep and food. One day, while moving a stone that was too heavy to lift, he pushed it with all his might;
at that moment, he attained a sudden and great enlightenment. He immediately composed a verse, saying: "I wish to investigate unsurpassed Bodhi..."

The Way: Swiftly clearing away the great mountain, one only knows it is no longer a mountain once one knows the Way. Turning back and leaping out of the Patriarch’s Barrier, he presented himself to Master Linshan.
Linshan certified him as a vessel of the Dharma. From birth, the Master was frail and weak; he could not even bear the weight of his own clothes.

During his time dwelling in the mountains, he exerted himself with utmost vigor to sharpen his resolve and remained steadfast. He personally engaged in farming, carving stone to clear fields without shrinking from toil or hardship.
He was unconcerned with his physical appearance; whenever he heard the clamor of the surrounding wilderness, he would say, "An old monk does not gather that which is inexhaustible."
He subsequently lived there without closing his door. He would often travel alone through the mountains at night;

once, when heavy snow had blocked the roads and he had been without food for several days, people urged him to shave his head, to which the Master replied, "I shall do so only when I have fully assumed the appearance of a monk. It was only then that he first shaved his hair, donned the dyed robes, and received full ordination.
From that time on, he did not venture beyond the mountain for twenty-four years, remaining as constant as a single day. At that time, in the city of Bao...
This was the former monastery of Chan Master Song Shibo. He invited the Master to restore it, and the Master accepted the summons.
First, he went to Ling Shan to sweep the master’s stupa, and only then departed. There is a verse that says: "Suddenly thirty years have passed; I have forgotten the path by which I came."
At that time, the Master was fifty-one years old; it was the Wanyili era, the year of Wuxu. While the Master resided at Baofang, his power of diligence increased ever more;
in all undertakings, he always took the lead by personal example. Though his body became withered and his bones stood bare, he never grew weary of the labor.
Thus, within a few years, hundreds of buildings were renovated, and several new sites were opened, including the Buddha Hall, the Main Gate, the Assembly Hall, and the Kitchen.

Everything was now complete. Monastics from the four quarters who had heard of his reputation arrived daily in increasing numbers. At that time, a monk asked, "Master, while residing on this mountain, have you ever met anyone of note?
The Master replied, "I have not yet traveled anywhere. The monk prodded him further, saying, "How can one view the world as small from a single corner?
The Master appreciated these words and, taking up his staff, set out on a long journey. He eventually reached the South Sea to visit Yunmen.

He retired to the Central Plains and entered Shaolin to pay homage at the stupa of the First Patriarch and seek out Master Wuyan as his spiritual mentor, inquiring about the meaning of the single transmission from the West.
Subsequently, he traveled to the capital to visit Chan Master Daguan, who held him in high esteem.

At that time, the great elders of the Dharma school all engaged with him in dialogue, none of whom failed to praise and commend him. Shortly thereafter, he went to Mount Wutai to study under Master Ruifeng.

Furthermore, the lineage of Master Feng was solitary and steep. Upon meeting him once, the Master attained realization and requested further instruction, saying, "I have doubts regarding several kōans involving the ancient worthies;
I beg the Master to provide guidance. Feng said, "Speak them. The Master said, "Linji said, 'The Buddha-dharma is not much.
What, then, is this? Feng said, "He told you it is not much. And what, then, is this?"
[The Master] said, "Mò. The Master said, "Xuansha said of Lingyun, 'I dare guarantee that you, elder brother, have not yet reached the ultimate.

Where is it that he has not yet reached the ultimate? Fēng said, "It is actually Xuansha who has not yet reached the ultimate. The Master said, "Zhaozhou said, 'The old woman at Mount Tai—I have thoroughly exposed her for you.
In what way was she exposed? Fēng said, "In fact, it was the old woman who exposed him."
Zhaozhou requested that Master Feng provide a verse. Feng said, "When you understand such a matter, simply let it be.

Zhaozhou bowed, and they were thus mutually sealed in realization. Master Feng then cross-examined Zhaozhou, and each answered with a verse; their words are recorded in a separate record. Zhaozhou’s verse says:

"The spring colors are hidden in the dark, The autumn light is revealed in the bright. Though one has eyes, there is nothing to discern; Though one employs wisdom, it is difficult to measure. Having reached home, one does not ascend to Chang’an."

On the road, he let the wind, flowers, snow, and moon take their course. Feng Shen approved of this; Master Guan’s words avoided total completion, his pivot valued mutual interplay, and they wondrously accorded with the tenets of Dongshan.
From then on, the Master’s heart grew weary of wandering, so he returned his staff to Baofang and began to open the hall to preach the Dharma.
At that time, Master Lai of Boshan served as the First Seat; the relationship between teacher and disciple was refined and harmonious.
He beat the drum of this Way and vigorously propagated its fundamental tenets. Monastic seekers from the four quarters arrived daily in increasing numbers.

In the year Wushen, the Shouchang Monastery of the district—which had been founded by the Chan Master Xizhu—had long fallen into ruin. The community requested the Master to reside there, and he accordingly accepted their invitation.

According to an old tradition, there was a prophecy that the Master’s birthplace and surname were identical to those of Master Zhu; thus, everyone regarded him as the reincarnation of Master Zhu. The Master...
He resided at Shouchang. Without seeking external support and without appointing a head of proselytization, he acted according to circumstances as required.
Within a few years, expenditures reached tens of thousands; yet his monastery became brilliantly adorned, and every detail necessary for a monastic grove was fully provided.

For twenty years, he has been surrounded by a thousand disciples, and he has also separately established more than twenty hermitages and temples. How could this not be because the Master acts through non-action?

Is he one who has been conjured by wondrous power? When the Master was born, his nature was upright and simple; his temperament was gentle yet his will was firm; his heart was harmonious yet his conduct was austere.

Though his limbs were not refined like the spokes of a wheel, his demeanor was dignified and solemn. Like the severity of frost or the warmth of the sun, he possessed a majesty that required no anger.
As soon as a monk beheld him, he lost his former self. In receiving others, he single-mindedly upheld the upward direction of the ancestral school.
In his conduct, he received requests for instruction from far and near as if they were silver mountains and iron walls; he never hastily granted approval to a single person.

Making authentic inquiry and earnest investigation his primary concern, those throughout the land heard only of his reputation, yet none could find a single word of concrete evidence upon which to rely as a pretext for criticism.
Such was his prudence and secrecy. Nevertheless, he maintained an extremely frugal lifestyle, to the point that some found his austerity unbearable.

The Master was serene and composed. Whenever he encountered a sick monk, he would invariably prepare the medicine and food himself. Upon the passing away of others, he would personally carry the firewood for the cremation.

In all matters concerning the monastic community, whether great or small, he applied his mind with thorough diligence. Without prior consultation, his actions accorded perfectly with the proper measure; he did not discriminate between the pure and the defiled, but exerted his full strength and heart in whatever he did.
His inner being was vast and expansive, as if his ears and eyes were oblivious to what they heard and saw. Thus it was when he grew old...
He grew increasingly vigorous; even at seventy, he still mingled with the ranks of laborers. He never ceased his work of plowing and digging, always departing before others and returning after them.

Preface and Eulogy for the Portrait of Master Wuming For a long time I have heard that the Master has been expounding the Dharma at Shouchang. The accounts of him passed down by the traveling monks have been confused and erroneous;
in short, they are all merely those who have caught sight of the shadow of the monastery’s flagpole. Recently, I traveled from Wuyue to pay my respects to the two great masters Zibo and Yunqi.

I returned to Kuangshan to plan for my life as a retired elder. Just then, the monk Wanshi arrived from Shouchang and recounted the circumstances of the Master’s entry into the room [for formal interview].
I joined my palms in praise, saying: "The Chan school has long been thin and weak; now, fortunately, we behold the Master’s bearing, which serves as a model for the ultimate Way.
Moreover, as this path is now reviving, those who are latecomers and juniors shall surely benefit."

This serves as a mirror for reflection; it is indeed a great fortune for the Dharma-gate that we must rely upon this. I am ashamed that I have long been submerged in the miasmic sea, unable to endure my suffering;
I have relegated the Way of Chan and the Buddha-dharma to the high shelves. How could I dare to place myself before others? I rejoice now to have the green mountains and white clouds as companions.

I am but a decaying bone, yet I consider myself to have understood this during my remaining years. I rejoice that there is one who upholds this Dharma-gate, though I regret not having had the opportunity to meet him in person.
I have thus briefly offered these humble praises to express my deep admiration.
I have long heard the name of ignorance, yet I have not seen the face of ignorance. Suddenly emerging from a great mountain, we see one another from across a thousand miles.
My livelihood lies at the head of my mattock; I preach the Dharma like a flash of lightning. I draw a bow without a string, accustomed to using the arrows of Shigong.
As soon as a person is shot, they flee at the sound of the string. Suddenly they collide with a stubborn stone, and the arrowhead and feathers are all shattered together.
A cast-iron ball is flung forth; those who see it are left without a thought or calculation. This is the venerable face-skin of my teacher;
looking at it, one may only realize it before words are spoken. If you ask about the direct and upward-moving pivot, the clouds and mountains fill the eyes, making them difficult to distinguish.
